posts.title: Can We Fast-Track New York City Out of the Housing Crisis?
posts.summary: Mayor Adams fast-tracks affordable housing approvals in 12 NYC districts by bypassing city council to speed development. However, an MIT economist's analysis found that upzoning increased built density by only 0.09 FAR over ten years on average, with building concentrated almost entirely in expensive neighborhoods with low existing density—most fast-track districts lack these economic conditions.
posts.text:
Have you signed up for my new product, Housing at Noon? Every morning I scour the news, Substacks, social posts, academic research, and economic data for interesting housing themes. I send a roundup of these themes—with my analysis and visualizations—to my subscribers at lunchtime. It's free. Sign up here. Now, on to today’s article…

Mayor Mamdani is sidelining the city council to fast-track affordable housing development in 12 New York City districts. Will it actually spur more building—and lower home prices and rents?

Zoning laws cap building heights across the city. But developers can ask for permission to build taller than regulations allow, as long as some portion of the new building contains “affordable” housing—units sold or rented to households whose incomes fall below some threshold of the area’s median.

In many city districts there has been limited uptake of this pathway. Part of the reason is that it’s expensive: such proposals need to go through the city’s elaborate review system, the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure, or ULURP. This takes time and money and often makes smaller projects unviable from the start.

But another reason developers likely hesitate to propose such projects is because of how thorny the review process is. In particular, the city council has to approve, and in practice, the entire council has deferred to the local council member in whose district the proposal would be built. That seems to have been enough to scare away at least some proje

posts.title: Why Did New Homes Stop Getting Bigger?
posts.summary: New American homes peaked at 2,467 square feet in 2015 but shrank to 2,142 square feet by 2025, reversing four decades of growth from 1,525 square feet in 1973. The author suggests builders downsized homes to attract first-time buyers and weaker-credit borrowers as prices climbed, particularly after 2015 when FHA loan insurance premiums were cut. Small houses under 1,200 square feet remain rare at just 5% of new homes today, down from 18% in 1978.
posts.text:
The typical new American house peaked at 2,467 square feet in 2015. By 2025 it had shrunk to 2,142 square feet. Before that, new houses had grown for four decades, from 1,525 square feet in 1973. The strip at the top of the chart shows the median size of a new house; the colored bands below show the share of new single-family houses built each year in each size range.

Small houses have barely come back. Houses under 1,200 square feet made up 18% of new homes in 1978 and just 2% in 2021; today they are 5%. Most of the shrinking has come from the largest houses getting smaller.

What’s driving this? To be honest, I’m not sure. Initially, I thought it could be a shift of construction, with more of it happening in places where homes tend to be smaller. But this of course flies against the trends: more homes are being built in the suburbs, and in the Sunbelt, where homes tend to be larger, not smaller.

Another idea: maybe lot sizes began shrinking, after having been boosted—not least by minimum lot size regulation—for decades. But this also doesn’t fit with the data: yes, lot sizes have been shrinking, but they’ve actually been falling since around 1990—far predating the turn towards smaller new homes.

Instead, what I think may be driving this is builders reaching for first-time buyers and borrowers with weaker credit, to keep sales up as prices climbed.

posts.title: Blue Cities Are Dense Cities
posts.summary: The post questions whether blue cities build housing slowly due to left-leaning politics or urban density. Using permitting data from 56 cities, the author finds that density alone explains 59% of variation in permitting times, while Democratic vote share explains only 19%—and adds nothing when density is included in the same model. The real constraint on housing is the inherent difficulty of building in dense cities, not political ideology.
posts.text:
In their book ‘Abundance’, Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson argue that we have less—and more expensive—goods and services (especially housing) than we would if we regulated industry less. They blame ‘blue states’ in particular, citing the association between left-leaning cities, more regulation, less housing supply, and high prices.

I think what Klein and Thompson are mostly picking up on is the nature of dense cities: they require more regulation than sparsely populated places, and they are more costly and difficult to build in. They’re also predominantly left-leaning.

But the causal association is between density and the difficulty of building, not democratic politics and the difficulty of building. As the chart below shows, the two are easily confounded because there is a strong association between density and politics.

When I posted this chart on social media, one commenter pointed me towards research which supposedly finds that political lean does help explain the failure to build—even after controlling for density and other metro-area characteristics (‘fixed effects’). The paper is called “Do liberal cities limit new housing development? Evidence from California” (Matthew Kahn, Journal of Urban Economics, 2011) and you can read it here.

But that paper actually proves my point: since it’s really hard to control for all the aspects of a city and tease out just political orientation, the author looks at changes over time: do cities that become more blue also become less p

posts.title: Product Launch: Housing at Noon
posts.summary: Sunderji launches Housing at Noon, a free weekday newsletter that synthesizes scattered housing news, data, and research into organized themes with analysis and charts. It targets housing professionals—agents, developers, researchers, investors, and journalists—delivering curated, data-driven insights at noon daily, emphasizing empirical evidence over generic headlines.
posts.text:
I’ve launched a new product called Housing at Noon. Every weekday, I survey the housing news, data, research, and online conversations from the previous 24 hours, then organize what matters into a handful of easy-to-read themes. I link to the original sources and add my own analysis, perspective, and relevant charts. It’s free.

Sign up here.

The housing conversation is scattered all over the place. A data point appears here, a piece of research there, followed by a useful observation on social media or a story in a trade publication. The pieces aren’t joined up, and it makes the big picture hard to absorb.

Housing at Noon is my attempt to make sense of that information flow each day.

Every weekday morning, I identify what is worth your attention, connect related ideas across different sources, and explain why they matter. I add Home Economics charts wherever they help contextualize the conversation, and email you the results at noon.

I genuinely believe Housing at Noon will help you stay better informed while spending less time reading the news and scrolling social media.

I want to emphasize that this isn’t a generic roundup of headlines—there are already plenty of those. posts.title: Cities are for the Young
posts.summary: Between 1970 and 2020, young adults (25-34) increased their share of downtown residents in major U.S. metros by 15 percentage points, while children halved from 26% to 12%. Economists found that proximity to restaurants and bars explained over 40% of this shift, driven largely by young people marrying and having children later in life.
posts.text:
Young adults have always been drawn to cities, and over the last 50 years they have become a much larger share of the people who live in them. Between 1970 and 2020, 25- to 34-year-olds’ share of residents within two miles of downtown in America’s 25 largest metros rose by 15 percentage points.

If the share of young adults increased, another group had to decrease—it was children. Within two miles of downtown, they fell from about one in four residents (26%) to one in eight (12%). Older residents held steady at about one in eight, even as they rose from one in ten Americans to one in six nationally.

The chart below shows these shifts for every age and distance. Teal means an age group became a larger share of local residents between 1970 and 2020; red means it became a smaller one. The darkest teal, people in their late 20s and early 30s within two miles of downtown, fades by about 10 miles out (roughly Washington Heights in Manhattan, or the Capital Beltway around Washington), where people in their 50s, 60s and 70s gain instead.

Why do young adults increasingly concentrate downtown? The most careful answer comes from economists Victor Couture and Jessie Handbury, who studied college graduates in large U.S. metros between 2000 and 2010 and tested the usual explanations against one another.

posts.title: Quality of Life Comes at a Cost
posts.summary: The post asks why housing is unaffordable in the world's most desirable cities. Data shows Monocle's top 20 quality-of-life cities have among the highest home price-to-income ratios globally. The author argues that while zoning regulations contribute, the core issue is systemic: high earners attracted to economically dynamic cities bid up land prices, making housing unaffordable regardless of location or building regulations.
posts.text:
The housing crisis is global. It is most acute in desirable cities that attract and produce highly skilled, high earning people. That’s my conclusion from juxtaposing the Monocle Magazine’s 2026 Quality of Life Survey—where they rank the top 20 cities in the world based on economic and cultural factors, from GDP to architecture—with Numbeo’s data on the cost of housing across major cities.

The chart below plots ~150 large cities according to Numbeo’s measure of their home price to income ratio. The most desirable 20 cities (according to Monocle) are colored blue. Almost all are among the most expensive cities in the world.

What can we learn from this?

For one, the explanation for the high cost of homes needs a global explanation. Yes: zoning, parking requirements, and restrictive floor-to-area ratios limit how much—and what kind of—housing can be built. These restrictions make our cities less dynamic, less walkable, and less diverse. But, to the extent these regulations vary in nature and intensity around the world, they cannot be the sole—or likely not even the primary—driver of housing unaffordability. We need a more systemic explanation for why housing is so out of reach for so many.

Monocle’s feature highlights just how pernicious the issue is across all kinds of cities, and not just those in Europe (numbers below indicate each city’s ranking on the global top 20):

2. Copenhagen — Monocle recommends the city drop “the restricted housing market” and stresses “ensuring

posts.title: 3 Reasons Higher Rates Aren’t an Imminent Problem
posts.summary: The post asks whether recent bond market selloffs pose an imminent economic threat. Sunderji argues they don't because: interest rates in most countries remain mid-range historically (US/UK/Australia above 4.75% but mid-tier against their own histories), the rate rise has been gradual (0.6 standard deviations monthly, versus the 1.5 threshold where stocks struggle), and stronger AI growth—rather than default risk—is driving increases.
posts.text:
I’m currently going through a phase of extreme news-aversion.

I’m sure this has something, maybe a lot, to do with coming back to my desk after a pretty relaxing summer. Since June, I’ve spent little time reading the news, and tried to spend much less time on social media. It feels like a good tradeoff: I feel marginally less informed but much more relaxed, creative, and focused.

So I was primed to take a skeptical stance towards recent headlines suggesting the bond market selloff imperils everything from economic growth to financial stability to stock markets (example: “Global Bond Selloff Sends Yields to the Highest Level Since 2008“).

The heatmap below visualizes interest rates across major economies over the past 35 years. Most are not especially high, either in absolute terms or versus their own histories. The chart places 16 of 18 countries in the middle third of their histories since 1990. Only Japan is top-third at 2.94%. Although interest rates in the US, UK and Australia exceed 4.75%, they remain mid-tier against their own histories.

This isn’t to say higher interest rates are not a problem. Many financial crises have been triggered by higher rates. Most governments are deeply indebted and, especially for emerging markets, the risk of sovereign defaults is rising (about 45% of OECD debt matures by 2027, with refinancing near twice the original coupon, per the OECD). posts.title: Where—and Why—have Rents Dropped?
posts.summary: The post examines why rents have dropped in certain U.S. cities, with Austin experiencing an 8% decline. Data shows net migration to Austin fell 65% (from 44K to 15K annually between 2021-2024), while large construction pipelines from the boom years continued delivering new housing through 2023-25. Rents declined most where migration slowed and building permits were highest, though remote work and tech employment proved poor explanatory factors.
posts.text:
Net domestic migration to Austin plummeted by 65%—from around 44K to 15K per year—between 2021 and 2024. This—and other variables reflecting both supply and demand—help explain why rents there are today 8% lower than a few years ago. The heatmap below visualizes these variables across cities. For example, darkly shaded cells under the “inflows” column represent cities where net migration decelerated sharply—these are clustered at the top of the chart, in cities where rents fell hardest.

The large pipeline of home construction was also clearly important. The explanatory power of supply is evident from the darkly shaded boxes at the top of the heatmap: rents fell most where many residential building permits were filed in 2021–23.

Other factors are also helpful in understanding where and by how much rents declined. In particular, rents dropped the most in places where valuations were high (where the home-price-to-income ratio was elevated in 2022 compared with the 15-year trailing average), and where migration decelerated (where the annual net domestic migration rate slowed between 2021–22 and 2023–25).

I’ve left the last two columns—the remote and tech shares of workers—to show that these are not great explanations of what’s happening (contrary to my hypothesis).

posts.title: Why did Home Prices and Rents Fall in Austin?
posts.summary: The post asks why Austin's home prices and rents fell despite apartment construction. Data shows the correlation between building permits and rents is unstable—mostly positive but negative during downturns. The author explains that demand shifts faster than supply; builders respond to rising demand with permits, but by the time construction completes 2-3 years later, demand has often weakened, causing prices to fall sharply in cities that built most.
posts.text:
A wave of apartment construction is widely cited as the reason home prices and rents in some cities—like Austin, TX—have fallen over the last few years. YIMBYs have pounced on the strong link between building permits and falling rents as vindication for their point of view: when cities add housing supply, rents drop.

If only it were so simple. The chart below shows the correlation between building permits and rents over time. It’s unstable. Most of the time, the correlation is positive. In other words, more building goes hand in hand with higher—not lower—prices and rents.

How can we explain this? Shouldn’t more housing supply lower prices?

Yes, in theory. Academic studies show that—holding everything else constant—adding supply to a market lowers prices and rents (though the magnitude of the effect is contested, see The Great Debate). But I’m talking about the real world, where nothing is constant.

In the real world, demand is moving at the same time as supply. The prices and quantities we observe are a function of both curves, and in practice—because demand moves faster and by more than supply—those prices and quantities are primarily a function of what’s happening on the demand side. These shifts in supply and demand occur in cycles.

How a typical cycle plays out

posts.title: Information Wants to be Free
posts.summary: The post asks whether information should cost a lot or be free. It shows that housing data, previously locked behind expensive paywalls, is becoming affordable: Parcl Labs provides 58,000+ NYC rental listings via API for $50/month, while the author's mapping tool costs $9/month—about one-fifth of competitors' prices. Meanwhile, 5.6 million business applications were filed in 2025, a record 60% higher than 2019.
posts.text:
The map below, which shows rents across New York City, was generated using property-level housing data from real estate data company Parcl Labs. I am not being compensated by the company (I’ll tell you if this changes), but am enthusiastic about sharing their product. I explain why below.

How much should information cost?

Maybe it should cost a lot, since a key piece of information can be the difference between making a good decision and a bad one. Or maybe it should be free—or close to free—since the cost of gathering and disseminating information tends towards zero1.

When it comes to economic data, “free” won the battle a long time ago. I don’t miss the Bloomberg terminal I had when I worked on Wall Street because the Fed’s free FRED data tool is excellent.

But in housing, private companies long ago gobbled up data and locked it up behind expensive paywalls. This has been a great business for firms like CoStar, who sell real estate data to institutions for thousands of dollars a month. For the rest of us, it’s been an impediment to making data-driven decisions.

This is now finally changing. The map above depicts rents around New York City. It’s based on more than 58,000 individual rental listings I was able to obtain using Parcl’s API, which starts at $50/month. If I was doing the same analysis in years past, I would have been limited to ZIP-level data from Zillow, and the map would be far less granular, interesting, and beautiful.

posts.title: Housing Research Needs a Credibility Revolution
posts.summary: The post asks why regulation-focused "YIMBY" housing studies dominate discourse despite being a minority view. Of 61 compiled papers, only one-third are YIMBY, yet these papers are cited 6 times more frequently than studies blaming high housing costs on income inequality and labor market geography. The author argues this citation imbalance reflects momentum rather than research quality, suggesting housing economics needs a "credibility revolution."
posts.text:
Academic studies which blame high housing costs on regulation have been cited 6x more widely than studies which come to other conclusions.

Why is housing so expensive? According to my compilation of the most widely cited economic papers over the past few decades about the housing crisis (The Great Debate, here), economists are split.

One camp—we might roughly call them YIMBY1 economists—argue that zoning, lot-size minimums, and height limits choke off new construction in the places people most want to live, so that prices are far above the cost of building. Those constraints, they argue, have priced workers out of the most productive cities and slowed the convergence of incomes across America.

But the majority of studies do not agree with this view—they instead blame high and increasingly unequal incomes competing for a limited set of desirable, high-productivity cities, the sorting of high earners into a handful of high-wage metros, and the high cost of scarce, well-located land.

Of the 61 papers in my compilation, only a third can be classified as YIMBY. But these have outsized influence: the average YIMBY paper has been cited 6x more than the average paper that comes to alternative explanations for the high price of housing.

Look for example at a typical YIMBY paper, like “The Economic Implications of Housing Supply” by Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko. The authors contend that “when housing supply is highly regulated in a certain metropolitan area, housing prices ar

posts.title: Manhattan is densifying again
posts.summary: The post asks whether Manhattan is densifying or declining. Data shows Manhattan's population density has reversed its 60-year decline: it added 108,000 people between 2010-2020 (its largest decade since 1900), lost 124,000 during the pandemic, but regained 77% by mid-2024, indicating densification is accelerating.
posts.text:
Most reporting about large coastal cities is pretty downbeat: stories about an exodus of families, deteriorating affordability, and decrepit public infrastructure. The adage “if it bleeds it leads” is as true as ever—alarmist, negative headlines simply grip attention more effectively than more optimistic stories.

But while looking for data to answer an entirely unrelated topic I stumbled across some data that tells an unapologetically positive story—about Manhattan no less, the subject of some of the most cynical stories about the decline of cities. The data shows that Manhattan is densifying, homes are being built, and the population is growing.

The maps above depict population density on the island since 1910. Three eras are evident.

First, de-densification during the 1910s-30s as urban slums emptied out and less densely parts of Manhattan and Brooklyn filled.

Second, more de-densification—but now led by families fleeing crime, in the 60s and 70s.

And the current, third era—beginning in the 1980s and only briefly interrupted by the pandemic—in which Manhattan is again becoming more dense. The trend is accelerating: Manhattan added 108,000 people between 2010 and 2020, its biggest decade of growth since the 1900s.

And although the pandemic reversed the trend1, that now looks like an interruption rather than a turning point. Manhattan lost 124,000 people between 2020 and 2021; by mid-2024 it had regained 77 percent of them.

posts.title: Cameron Murray's Unconventional Take on Housing
posts.summary: This post doesn't present a traditional data analysis or specific findings with numbers. Instead, it's an introduction to a podcast/video interview with Cameron Murray, an Australian housing economist who challenges mainstream housing experts like Ed Glaeser on causes and solutions to the housing crisis. The post outlines discussion topics ranging from zoning's role in housing affordability to treating housing as a financial asset, without presenting quantitative results or key statistics.
posts.text:
I sat down with Cameron Murray late last night to talk about housing (he’s based in Brisbane, Australia—bridging our 14 hour time difference is always a challenge).

Cameron is a controversial figure in the housing world. He thinks some of the most respected intellectual giants of the field—people like Ed Glaeser, for example—are completely and utterly wrong about the nature of, and solutions for, the housing crisis.

Australians—like Canadians (my nationality)—have a reputation for speaking plainly, and Cam is a good example. He seethes with disdain for a lot of the nonsense written about housing, on social media and in the mainstream press. I mostly agree with him.

Regardless of whether you agree with him, listening to Cam talk about housing is often thought-provoking and always entertaining.

I hope you enjoy our conversation.

posts.title: Is Solving the Housing Crisis Really Simple?
posts.summary: The post asks whether upzoning alone can solve the housing crisis. Sunderji argues housing affordability is primarily driven by income inequality rather than zoning restrictions, citing data showing prices are high where incomes are high, immigration impacts costs more than zoning, and building rises when prices rise. He presents economists' competing views to demonstrate the issue's complexity rather than the "simple" supply-side solution YIMBYs propose.
posts.text:
Why is housing so expensive? How can we make it more affordable?

It depends who you ask. The conventional view is that regulation is to blame; our major cities are zoned for single-family housing—this prevents us from building more homes and lowering prices. In the conventional view, the solution is to ‘upzone’—allow denser housing to be built in these expensive cities.

To me, a more accurate description of the issue is that housing is a “normal good” (we tend to want more of it when our incomes increase), and a “positional good” (it’s distributed across the population according to income), and that—amidst steeper income inequality—those at the very bottom of the ladder are having a tough time getting as much housing as they need.

In my view, upzoning is a worthy goal, but only because it will make cities more dynamic. I think it will do little for prices. To the degree a housing crisis exists, it’s a function of wealth and income inequality.

Housing is in many ways similar to other human rights, like education and healthcare—not least, it’s hard to boost supply. For education and healthcare that’s due to Baumol’s cost disease, while for housing it’s mostly about economics and geography. But the remedy is the same: subsidize the neediest households.

When I publicize my view, in this newsletter or on social media, I often get a barrage of rebuttals. One of the most frequent is “don’t make it so complicated…the solution is simple: we need to upzone! It’s Econ 101.”

The data shows an urban-to-suburban shift over the past five years, with population density, commute times, and homeownership patterns explaining the trend. posts.text:
Since the pandemic, the urban cores of most large U.S. metros have lost ground to their suburbs and exurbs—both in population and in home-price growth.

It’s a story best told visually, with maps. But no single, static map can hold its complexity.

That’s where ProMap—the tool I released last week—comes in. In this short video, I use it to trace New York City’s urban-to-suburban shift over the past five years. I show how population density, commute times, and homeownership help explain this phenomenon.

posts.title: A Rising Tide is not Lifting All Boats
posts.summary: The post asks whether luxury home sales are booming across all metros or just some. Data shows that while prices rose 66-68% in Philadelphia and Atlanta since 2019, the share of genuinely luxury sales (homes outrunning their market's appreciation) actually fell from 10% to 7-8%—contrasting with Miami's luxury boom. This reflects a "K-shaped" economy where affordable mid-market sales dominate these metros rather than high-end transactions.
posts.text:
The luxury boom is dominating the headlines but in some metros the market is actually moving the other way. In Atlanta and Philadelphia, for example, a shrinking share of what sells is genuinely high-end, even as prices climb. These are affordability-driven markets, where the deals are getting done in the middle and at the bottom, not at the top.

Teasing out the proportion of luxury transactions is surprisingly tricky. You could define it using a fixed dollar threshold—say, homes over $1 million—but over time a rising share of homes will fall into the luxury category just because of generally rising prices.

Or, you could define luxury as some arbitrary top proportion of priciest homes. For example Redfin’s luxury index defines luxury as the top 5%. But this isn’t helpful for figuring out what proportion of sales are luxury: by construction, in Redfin’s definition, luxury will always comprise 5% of sales.

Here’s how I measure it: I set each metro’s luxury line at its 2019 top-decile sale price, then float that line up in step with local prices, so a home only counts as luxury if it outruns its own market. When the share of sales above that floating line falls, the market is genuinely moving down-market.

The clearest cases are Philadelphia and Atlanta, and they are striking because both appreciated hard. Prices rose 66% in Philadelphia and 68% in Atlanta since 2019 (the strongest gains after Miami). Yet their real luxury share fell from about 10% to 7% and 8% respectively —

posts.title: Claude Code for Research: Preventing Hallucinations
posts.summary: The post asks how researchers can safely use Claude Code despite its tendency to fabricate information. Sunderji presents three guardrails: maintaining a data lake that forces the AI to cite specific sources, running background research that requires URLs and verbatim quotes for every claim, and conducting final fact-checks against verified data. He reports these methods have prevented fabrications across roughly 80 research briefings over the past year.
posts.text:
Anyone who has used Claude Code for more than a few minutes knows that—just like any other AI tool—even this formidable machine shares the same penchant for fabrications. Does this mean serious researchers shouldn’t use Claude Code? Not in my view.

I notice it most with a fresh instance of Claude Code, one without the elaborate guardrails I’ve imposed on the version I use daily. It just…makes stuff up. And the fabrications are so believable that only constant insistence that the model verify itself will surface them.

These convincing fabrications might be fine for casual users—if what the model says is that plausible, it’s probably not far from the consensus. But for research, where made-up results are embarrassing at best and career-ending at worst, they’re unacceptable.

Does this mean serious researchers shouldn’t use Claude Code? Not in my view. It just requires imposing strict rules, workflows, and audits along the way—not so different from the precautions any senior researcher takes with a junior colleague, though the form has to be tailored to the tool.

Here are three of the ways I keep Claude Code on guardrails while researching the housing market for Home Economics.

One: Data Lake

The single best way to stop Claude Code fabricating results is to point it at a specific source it must draw its conclusions from. For me that’s my data lake—nothing more complex than a (very big) folder in the cloud. I use Dropbox for its file-version history: useful for the rare but

posts.title: The Luxury Boom Is Real—But Only in 2 Cities
posts.summary: The post asks whether a genuine luxury housing boom exists or if rising prices just make all homes seem more expensive. Data shows a real luxury shift in only two cities: San Jose's luxury share jumped from 10% to 17% (2019-2026), driven by AI wealth, while Miami's rose from low levels to a larger share, driven by finance migration. Most other major metros show no shift toward luxury homes.
posts.text:
The housing market shows evidence of American wealth pooling disproportionately in two cities—San Jose/San Francisco and Miami. In these cities the housing market is genuinely shifting upmarket: a rising share of sales are high-end.

Identifying a genuine shift to luxury is harder than it sounds, because the obvious yardsticks both fail. If you use a fixed dollar threshold—say, homes over $3 million—the luxury share will seem to rise as prices climb for the whole market, even without any real bias towards high end sales.

You could define luxury as a fixed share of the market. Redfin’s luxury index for example defines luxury as the top 5% by price. But then you will, by construction, find that luxury always equals 5% of sales—and so can never register a shift at all.

Here’s how I distinguish a real shift to luxury from ordinary appreciation: I set each metro’s luxury threshold at its 2019 top-decile sale price, then float that line upwards in step with local prices. As a result, a home only counts as luxury if it outruns the market.

The map below plots each luxury sale in Silicon Valley and the Bay Area over the last 12 months as a spike. The tallest stacks run in a tight corridor from San Francisco down the Peninsula through San Mateo and Palo Alto into San Jose; across the East Bay and the valley’s edges the spikes are short and scattered. The Bay Area’s luxury market, in other words, is a few square miles.

posts.title: Introducing ProMap
posts.summary: Aziz Sunderji introduces ProMap, a tool addressing how traditional maps misrepresent housing data by overweighting large geographic areas and using poorly-calibrated color gradients. ProMap uses population-sized dots for ZIP codes, allowing users to color-code by price level or change, zoom, search, and compare specific regions. The redesigned tool is free with premium features available via subscription ($9/month or $7.50/month annually).
posts.text:
Maps are hard to get right.

Most give too much weight to geographically large areas instead of populous ones. And on the most common kind of price map—the choropleth, where regions are shaded by a variable like home prices—a color gradient tuned for the national level falls apart at the local one.

I built ProMap to solve both of these challenges:

Each dot is a ZIP code, sized to its population

Each dot is colored by your choice of either price level or price change

Pan, zoom, and search

Re-color the ZIPs in view relative to each other

Draw a boundary around the specific ZIPs you want to compare

Works seamlessly on mobile; easily share on social media

Watch a demo video here.Try the new ProMap here.

posts.title: An Exodus of Children from New York City
posts.summary: New York City lost 150,000 children (9%) between 2020-2024, primarily due to families migrating to suburbs like Nassau County and beyond. While international migration replaced about a third of these losses, the suburbs themselves are also losing children overall because births don't offset aging, except in Rockland and Ocean counties with growing Orthodox communities.
posts.text:
Today there are 150,000 fewer children living in New York City than on the eve of the pandemic—a nearly 9% drop. For context, the five boroughs lost three-and-a-half times as many kids in the four years after 2020 as they did in the preceding ten. The number of children in the city had been on a volatile but downward path since peaking in 2000, but the past few years have seen a collapse.

Although fertility is having a moment, that’s not the mechanism behind the city’s kid decline. Between 2020 and 2024 the five boroughs had roughly 372,000 births and 355,000 children aging out of childhood—a net gain of about 17,000 from natural change alone.

The reason New York is losing kids is migration. Families are fleeing—primarily to the suburbs. The most popular destination is Nassau County, on Long Island, which absorbed nearly one in ten kids who left the city. Westchester took 5%. Fairfield County in Connecticut and Suffolk—the more distant of Long Island’s two big suburb counties—each captured roughly 3.5%. The three nearest New Jersey counties (Bergen, Hudson, Essex) absorbed another 3% each. The remaining smaller MSA suburbs collectively captured another 9%.

The number of families moving further afield is surprisingly high. About 60% of kids leaving New York City moved outside commuting distance of the city. posts.title: What’s Driving City-to-Suburb Migration?
posts.summary: Two datasets on families leaving New York City for suburbs challenge the affordability argument. Census data from ~200 movers shows zero cited housing costs as the primary reason, instead citing "better housing" and "more space." A NYC Department of Education survey of 2,000 families ranked cheaper housing fifth (33%), behind "better environment for kids" (64%), "more space" (50%), and school/crime concerns, suggesting space availability, not cost, drives city-to-suburb migration.
posts.text:
My favorite data journalist John Burn-Murdoch at The Financial Times has sparked another round of hand wringing about declining fertility—and in doing so, has reignited a long running complaint from housing advocates: the reason people are having fewer babies is because it’s too expensive. In their telling, housing is the main driver of this expense, and NIMBYism is the root of it: cities don’t permit enough housing and this drives costs up—and families out.

But the data suggests that families are leaving cities not pushed out by affordability, but lured by the attraction of the suburbs—particularly the plentiful space they offer. At least, that’s what the data from New York City suggests.

We have two good datasets here. One comes from the Census Bureau, and asks households who moved in the past year about their reasons for moving.

When we filter for those who have children and who moved from New York City to nearby suburbs, housing affordability doesn’t appear once in the data as the primary reason for moving (even though it’s an option). Instead, movers cite “better housing”, “wanted to own”, “easier commute”, and “marital status change” as the motivations.

This is an admittedly thin dataset, with only about 200 families who meet our criteria being tracked, but it’s telling that not one placed affordability as the main reason for leaving the city for the suburbs.

posts.title: Miami got NYC’s billionaires. Will it get their businesses?
posts.summary: Since 2020, wealthy New Yorkers have fled to Miami at unprecedented rates, with $5 billion in taxable income leaving NYC for Miami in 2020-21 versus only $500 million moving the opposite direction. The exodus is concentrated among the ultra-wealthy: the mean income of New York migrants to Florida jumped from $120,000 in 2018 to $223,000 in 2020-21, more than double those who stayed.
posts.text:
This is an excerpt from an article I published in the Financial Times earlier this week. You can read the whole article here (and feel free to leave a supportive comment!).

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani is threatening a pied-à-terre tax on high-priced homes owned by non-residents. He has made Citadel boss Ken Griffin the poster child for the tax’s targets. In response, Griffin is threatening to shutter work on Citadel’s $6bn new office development on Park Ave.

This back-and-forth is how the city works: it offers unparalleled access to deep pools of capital and human talent, but takes its pound of flesh from the companies and high earners based here. They complain about each other, but life goes on; those high earners constantly threaten to leave, but they rarely do.

So it must have felt like low-risk populism for New York Governor Hochul, speaking at a campaign rally in 2022, to tell prospective tax refugees:

Just jump on a bus and head down to Florida where you belong, OK. Get outta town. Get outta town. Because you don’t represent our values. You are not New Yorkers.

She probably didn’t expect so many to heed her advice (though they took private jets, not buses). Since Jan 2020, there’s been an exodus of financial titans flocking to Miami. Some of the high-profile departees include Carl Icahn (Icahn Enterprises), Paul Singer (Elliott Management), Barry Sternlicht (Starwood Capital), Cathie Wood (ARK Invest), and Daniel Sundheim (D1 Capital).

posts.title: The Midwest's Brain Drain Is Accelerating
posts.summary: The Midwest's domestic migration improved from losing 175K people annually in 2021 to gaining 16K in 2025, but this masks a troubling trend: fewer people are leaving (outflows dropped 125K), not more arriving. Critically, the region's natural population increase collapsed from +240K annually in 2014 to +50K in 2024, while out-migrants are increasingly high-earning and educated—those earning over $200K increased by 54K annually in Illinois alone—leaving behind lower-income residents who can't afford to leave.
posts.text:
The Midwest is having a moment, with many pointing out that the region went from losing 175K people per year in 2021 to gaining 16K in 2025—its first positive year of domestic net migration in well over a decade. The conventional reading is that this marks the start of an affordability-driven comeback: coastal housing refugees are discovering the amenities of Cleveland and other Midwest cities, especially since the Sun belt is no longer a beacon of affordability.

But the decomposition of the flows tells a different story. The improvement is not because more people are arriving, it’s because fewer are leaving. Inflows have been rangebound for a decade around 770K per year. The swing is entirely from outflows: 125K fewer people left Midwestern states in 2024 than in 2021.

Why are fewer people leaving the Midwest?

It might well be affordability. The median home in the Midwest costs around $265K—the lowest of any region by roughly $50K. The biggest drop in outbound migration from the Midwest was to California where—amid spiraling housing costs—flows fell from 89K a year in 2014–18 to 58K in 2024 (the most recent year of Census data in which net migration is broken down into inflows and outflows). It’s families with kids, who are more impacted by housing affordability, who are leaving much less than before.

posts.title: Dads are doing more childcare—and they love it
posts.summary:
# Summary

American fathers today spend over 80 minutes daily on childcare—more than triple the 30 minutes their Boomer fathers spent in 1965—by reducing work hours and TV time. The article explores why this dramatic shift occurred, arguing that while women's workforce entry played a role, the steepest increases happened decades later (1990s-2000s), suggesting fathers increasingly view childcare as rewarding leisure rather than mere obligation.
posts.text:
This is an article I co-wrote with Derek Thompson. You may know Derek from his 17-year stint as a columnist at The Atlantic, where he remains a contributing writer, from his bestselling book Abundance (co-written with Ezra Klein and published last year), or from his excellent podcast Plain English. Derek and I met in the most inhuman way—on X.com—but bonded over the most human of things: we are both fathers to young children. Naturally, the subject of our collaboration—modern fatherhood—hits close to home for both of us. We hope you like it.

American fatherhood has transformed in the last few generations. Compared to their Boomer parents, childcare time among Millennial dads has more than doubled. Compared to their Silent Generation grandparents, it’s nearly quadrupled. You will be hard-pressed to find any part of day-to-day modern life that has changed more in the last half-century than the way today’s parents—and fathers, in particular—spend their time.

In 1965, the typical married father barely spent half an hour each day actively engaged in childcare, according to the best time-use data we have1. Today, Millennial thirty-something dads typically spend more than 80 daily minutes changing diapers, reading and playing with their children, driving them to soccer practice, and going over homework. posts.title: When's the Best Time to Buy a Home?
posts.summary: The post asks when buyers should purchase homes, analyzing the trade-off between selection and price. Data from 45 U.S. metros shows fresh inventory peaks in late April (35% above January levels), while buyer leverage peaks in late October-November. Buyers must choose between spring's selection or fall's better deals, with regional variations significant.
posts.text:
This is the final installment of analysis I co-authored in collaboration with the research team at RedFin (a national real estate brokerage).

Buyers face a trade-off that sellers don’t: the time of year for selection is not the best time of year for deals. That’s the conclusion from a recent analysis I co-authored with the research team at Redfin.

The chart below shows two seasonal patterns across 45 large U.S. metros, each tracked through the calendar year. Each bubble is a metro, sized by its sales volume. The top panel measures fresh inventory—how many new homes hit the market relative to that metro’s annual average. The bottom panel measures buyer leverage—how much, on average, sellers concede off their original asking price. Both panels are scaled so “up” is better for the buyer.

The two peaks don’t line up. Fresh inventory peaks in early summer. In fact, prospective buyers with very specific requirements will want to be in the market even earlier—when new listings surge—which is in late April. On the other hand—for those seeking deals—buyer leverage peaks four months later, in late October and November.

The seasonal swing in selection is large. Fresh listings in late January run 35% below the annual average—a July buyer sees nearly twice the new inventory of a January buyer.

posts.title: Late April Is the Best Time to List a Home For Sale
posts.summary: Homes listed in late April sell faster and for more money than other times of year. Sellers listing in late April's final week see sale-to-list ratios peak, close deals 17% more often within two weeks, and spend 9% fewer days on market. However, the optimal listing time varies significantly across metros, ranging from mid-March to mid-June.
posts.text:
This week I am publishing articles I co-wrote in collaboration with the research team at RedFin (a national real estate brokerage).

Homes listed in late April sell faster and for more money than those listed at other times of the year. That’s the conclusion from a recent analysis I wrote in collaboration with the research team at Redfin.

The chart below shows four metrics arranged like clocks, with January at the top. The thickness of the lines indicates how active the market is at each time of year (based on the number of new listings). The color of the line indicates how high the metric is compared to its average. So, for example, the top-left radar chart has a thick blue line in late April—this means that, at that time of year, the market is active and more homes are selling above list than usual.

All four clocks bulge in the same late-April zone—that’s the best time to sell.

Sellers who list in the last week of April see sale-to-list ratios peak, move homes under contract within two weeks 17% more often, and spend 9% fewer days on market than the yearly average.

Competing supply (total active listings) is roughly 8% below the late-summer peak, so each listing faces fewer rival homes.

The worst stretch, across every one of the four metrics, is the gap between Thanksgiving and Christmas.

posts.title: Seasonality in American Housing
posts.summary: The post asks whether housing market seasonality varies by region. Data shows seasonal listing swings are smallest in warm-weather metros like Tampa, Miami, and Phoenix, but largest in San Francisco, Boston, and Seattle. Supply constraints, not just weather, drive seasonality—the Bay Area's limited inventory creates intense seasonal competition despite mild winters.
posts.text:
This week I will be publishing articles I co-wrote in collaboration with the research team at RedFin (a national real estate brokerage).

The best time to buy or sell a home varies from metro to metro, but the swings are bigger in some parts of the U.S. than others. In the southern part of the country, where weather tends to be warmer, the swing in how many new listings hit the market by season is fairly small. In the northern part of the country, which has more extreme weather, the swing in new listings is bigger.

Another important factor is supply: Highly populated areas with limited supply tend to be more seasonal.

The metros with the least seasonal housing markets, i.e. where the seasonal swing in listings is smaller, are in Florida. Tampa is the least seasonal of all. Next come Fort Lauderdale, Miami, West Palm Beach and Orlando . The next two are also located in places with warm weather throughout the year: Phoenix and Las Vegas.

On the other end of the spectrum, the places with the most seasonal metros are either in colder climates—or they’re in the Bay Area. San Francisco has the most seasonal market in the nation. Next come Boston, Seattle, San Jose, CA and Minneapolis.

“The fact that the Bay Area has the most seasonal housing market shows that seasonality isn’t just about weather–it’s also about supply,” said Asad Khan, a senior economist at Redfin. “In places like San Francisco and San Jose, where there are a lot of house hunters and limited inventory, timing m

posts.title: AI has a PR problem
posts.summary: Americans strongly distrust AI: 57% believe its risks outweigh benefits, and only 32% trust it, below the 49% global average. The post attributes this partly to tech's extreme geographic concentration—three California counties hold more tech payroll than 3,100 others combined—making the industry feel like a "coastal elite activity" disconnected from most of America.
posts.text:
People are trying to kill Sam Altman. Early on Friday morning, a 20-year-old man threw a Molotov cocktail at the OpenAI CEO’s home, setting off a small fire near the front gate. He later turned up at the OpenAI office and threatened to burn down the building. Then on Sunday, a young couple in a moving car fired a shotgun at Altman’s home.

The incidents are extreme but the sentiment is not. Americans really dislike AI. A March NBC News poll found that 57% of Americans believe the risks of AI outweigh the benefits. The Edelman Trust Barometer puts American trust in AI at just 32%, well below the global average of 49%. Even among Gen Z, Gallup found anger toward AI up nine points year-over-year and excitement down fourteen.

Some of this is self-inflicted. AI firms have spent two years competing to describe their own products as the most existentially dangerous. But the industry’s geographic isolation from the rest of the country doesn’t help.

The maps below compare the geographic locations of company payrolls across three industries of roughly equal size (~$600 billion each). Each bubble represents the size of the payroll in that county. Construction and retail fill the map. But tech’s presence is disproportionately concentrated in a few counties on the California coast, in New York, and in smaller clusters in DC and Boston. Three California counties — Santa Clara, San Mateo, and San Francisco — account for more tech payroll than the bottom 3,100 counties combined.

posts.title: Is High Immigration Making Us Unhappy?
posts.summary:
# Summary

The post asks whether high immigration explains declining happiness in Western countries over the past five years. Data from 30 OECD countries shows richer nations experienced the largest immigration surges (10+ per 1,000 people annually) and have seen the steepest happiness declines, while happiness levels are converging globally—but the author notes this correlation doesn't establish causation, as happiness drops persist even after controlling for economic and social factors.
posts.text:
Western countries have experienced a precipitous slide in happiness over the past 5 years. The drop has been steepest in English-speaking countries. Why?

Last week I showed that rising housing unaffordability is not the explanation. The reception to that piece was interesting. On X, amid a flurry of racist comments (a favorite seems to be “the problem is too many Azizs”) were some more measured arguments that high levels of immigration might be to blame.

Is surging immigration the explanation for declining happiness?

The heatmap below provides some context. It charts the relationship between a number of different variables for 30 countries in the OECD (Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development; a club of mostly wealthy democracies):

GDP per capita: countries are ranked from richest to poorest

Happiness: cells are colored by the level of happiness and direction of change; a dot denotes the year of peak happiness for each country

Immigration: years in which any country experienced high immigration inflows—defined as more than 10 people per 1,000—are outlined with dotted lines. More than 15 per 1,000 is denoted by a solid outline

This is one of the most information-dense visualizations I have ever produced—but I promise it rewards study. Here are 5 observations you might take from this chart.

I. Richer countries are generally happier

posts.title: English speaking countries are miserable
posts.summary: Why are English-speaking countries becoming unhappy? The World Happiness Report 2026 shows life satisfaction has declined in the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and U.K. since 2006, with under-25s ranking 122nd-133rd out of 136 countries. While housing affordability is often blamed, data shows no meaningful correlation—it explains just 6% of happiness variation. Countries like Estonia and Latvia experienced similar housing cost increases yet saw happiness rise sharply, suggesting other factors are responsible.
posts.text:
The Anglosphere has grown unhappy. The World Happiness Report 2026 found that life satisfaction has declined in the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the U.K. since 2006. The drop is especially acute among the young: under-25s in these countries rank between 122nd and 133rd out of 136 countries for changes in happiness, with life evaluations falling roughly twice as much as the population average. Among the 37 OECD nations, Canada has slid from 5th to 18th since 2011; the U.K. from 15th to 20th. For the second year running, no English-speaking country ranks in the top 10. Why?

One of the more prominent explanations is housing. Home prices relative to incomes have surged across the Anglosphere, and the hypothesis—advanced by Noah Smith, Matt Yglesias, Ezra Klein, the IMF, and Gallup among others—is that unaffordable housing is to blame for plummeting life satisfaction. Does this hold up?

To find out, I matched the OECD’s price-to-income index with the World Happiness Report’s happiness scores and measured the changes in each over the last decade. The chart below plots this relationship.

If this chart looks to you like a random scattering of bubbles, you’re not wrong: there is no meaningful correlation between rising housing costs and declining happiness. Housing affordability explains just 6% of the variation in happiness, and is not statistically significant.

posts.title: The Immigration Backlash is a Global Phenomenon
posts.summary: The post asks whether the US immigration backlash is uniquely American. Data from nine countries shows a synchronized global pattern: net migration surged post-pandemic (peaking at 7.2 million collectively in 2023) then reversed sharply by 2025 (to 1.3 million). Despite different policy approaches, all nine countries experienced similar cycles driven by labor shortages and followed by public backlash, with the US surge actually being milder per capita than Canada or Australia.
posts.text:
Americans have a habit of assuming that whatever is happening in the United States is unique to the United States. The immigration crackdown is the latest example. Census data released this year showed net international migration fell 54%, from 2.7 million to 1.3 million. The New York Times covered it as a Trump story. But the chart below shows that nine countries on three continents experienced the same post-pandemic immigration surge and the same sharp reversal—most of it before Trump took office.

Despite widespread criticism of the Biden administration for lax border enforcement, the US immigration surge, measured per capita, was actually the mildest of the nine. The US migration figures use CBO estimates, which are higher than official Census counts because they include undocumented migrants. Even so, at its 2023 peak, US net migration ran at about 10 per thousand—one-third of Canada’s rate (31.5) and half of Australia’s (21).

And despite the strongarm tactics of the Trump administration, the US decline was also comparatively gentle: net migration fell 88% from peak, but from a lower height. Canada’s net migration swung from the highest rate among the nine to outright population decline in 2025—the first in modern Canadian history. The UK fell 78% from peak. New Zealand fell 87%.

posts.title: The dominoes that delay homeownership
posts.summary: The post asks why first-time homebuyers are older now than before. Data shows the median age of first-time homebuyers has risen eight years, but this isn't primarily due to affordability fluctuations. Instead, Americans are hitting every life milestone later—living at home longer, delaying independent renting, postponing marriage, and waiting longer before buying homes.
posts.text:
I am running a 30 minute Claude Code teach-in tomorrow at noon over Zoom. Join me (it’s free)—just hit ‘reply’ and tell me about the work you do and why you’d like to learn about Claude Code.

Why are people buying their first home later in life? Housing affordability is at a low point right now, and this is surely forcing some young buyers to wait. But the first-time buyer age has only gone one way over time: up—and that’s happened even as affordability has waxed and waned.

A better explanation is that Americans are doing everything later in life. The chart below plots the time the average American spends living at home, living independently as a single renter, married and renting, and married and owning. The median age at which people transition between these states is labeled. The eight-year rise in first-time buyer age is the cumulative effect of reaching every prior milestone later in life.

posts.title: How a $500K Family in Manhattan Actually Lives
posts.summary: The New York Times featured a $500K-earning Manhattan couple living in a cramped 800 sq ft apartment paying $3,900/month rent, sparking outrage from readers. However, census data shows typical households at their income level in Manhattan pay $6,000/month rent for a 2-bedroom apartment while still saving $4,000+ monthly, suggesting the couple made unusually austere financial choices rather than facing genuine constraints.
posts.text:
I am running a 30 minute Claude Code teach-in on Friday at noon over Zoom. Join me (it’s free)—just hit ‘reply’ and tell me about the work you do and why you’d like to learn about Claude Code.

Earlier this week, the New York Times published an article titled How a Family of 3 Lives on $500,000 on the Upper West Side. The NYT is read by 15x more Americans who live outside New York City than within it, many of them with incomes closer to the national median of $80k than $500k. So the most common response was to dunk on a place where apparently even a couple earning half a million dollars are reduced to living in a cramped 800 square foot apartment, Maltese poodle at their feet, baby in a crib in the same room—separated by a curtain. A typical comment read: “Half a million dollars and living like that? Knock yourself out.”

But in fact, the couple featured in the article, Anala Gossai and Brendon O’Leary, have made some bizarrely austere financial decisions. Most acutely: their small 1-bedroom apartment, for which they pay $3,900 per month, allowing them to set aside $10k in savings per month. Census Data shows that, in 2024, in Manhattan, the typical household at their income level with one child lives in a 2-bedroom apartment and pays $6k in rent (in the couple’s specific neighborhood it’s even higher—$7,700).

posts.title: First-Time Home Buyers Are Older Than Ever
posts.summary: Using University of Michigan longitudinal data tracking 85,000 individuals since 1968, the post asks at what age people buy their first home. It finds the median first-time buyer is now 35—three years older than a decade ago and eight years older than the 1970s. The analysis reveals the Federal Reserve's widely cited data underestimates this trend due to methodological biases.
posts.text:
I am running a 30 minute Claude Code teach-in on Friday at noon over Zoom. Join me (it’s free)—just hit ‘reply’ and tell me about the work you do and why you’d like to learn about Claude Code.

At what age do people buy their first home? My analysis of data from the University of Michigan’s Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) shows that, on average, they’re 35—three years older than a decade ago, and eight years older than in the 1970s.

The PSID is a remarkable dataset. Like wildlife researchers tagging a pod of whales, the researchers at the University of Michigan have tracked 85,000 individuals from 5,000 families they began studying in 1968.

This ‘longitudinal’ data allows us to observe the kids in these families as they leave home, form their own households, rent their first apartments, and eventually become first time buyers (FTBs) of homes. And because specific individuals are tracked over time, we can pinpoint the exact moment someone transitions from renting to owning for the first time, and how old they were when it happened. No other U.S. dataset can do this, and none go as far back as the 1960s.

It might seem obvious that people are buying their first home at an older age. After all, young Americans are achieving all the hallmarks of adulthood—from getting their driver’s licenses, moving out of their parents’ homes, getting jobs, to getting married and having kids—later than prior generations. Why would buying their first home be any different?

posts.title: Statistical Annex to ‘First Time Home Buyers Really Are Older’
posts.summary: The post asks whether the Federal Reserve's measure of first-time homebuyers accurately identifies them. The data shows significant misclassification: the CCP definition misses prior owners whose old mortgages aren't reported by creditors, including roughly 1 million "boomerang" buyers per year (32% of rent-to-own transitions) plus owners with paid-off or cash-purchased homes—all older than true first-timers—inflating reported FTB ages.
posts.text:
1. How the Fed measures first-time buyers

The NY Fed’s Consumer Credit Panel (CCP) is a 5% random sample of all Americans with an Equifax credit report, drawn quarterly since Q1 1999 (Lee & van der Klaauw, Staff Report 479, 2010). It contains approximately 14.2 million individuals as of 2023.

The Fed defines a first-time buyer as someone whose credit report shows “the first appearance of an active mortgage since 1999 with no indication of any prior closed mortgages on the borrower’s credit report” (Lee & Tracy, 2019). In their February 2025 update, they state it more simply: “We identify FTBs as households that have never had a mortgage lien.” They also explicitly assume “no FTB makes an all-cash purchase.”

The CCP is purely credit data—it tracks debt accounts, not homeownership status. It has no concept of “owner” or “renter.” It knows only whether someone has or has had a mortgage.

posts.title: An Easy Way to Look at Housing Data
posts.summary: The post introduces Metro Housing Explorer, a free tool for analyzing housing metrics across 933 U.S. metro areas. Using Austin as an example, it shows median prices peaked at $554K in mid-2022 (up 52% from pre-pandemic), then fell 24% to $420K with a 6% year-over-year decline. Active inventory surged 166% to 11,803 listings, while homes now sit 110 days on market versus 29 days five years ago—making Austin's market among America's slowest.
posts.text:
Link: Home Economics Metro Housing Data Explorer. Search any of 933 U.S. metro areas—it’s free.

There is a lot of housing content on social media. Most of it consists of some metric (price, inventory, etc.)—either charted, or displayed in a map. Yet, it’s surprisingly hard to generate those images, and especially hard to make them look good.

Two weeks ago I released an updated version of my mapping tool. Today I am sharing another tool that puts high quality data at your fingertips, in a beautiful and easy-to-share format.

Metro Housing Explorer lets you view any metric of your choice, from price to inventory to months of supply, for any city. Prices are sourced from Zillow, and all other metrics come from Redfin.

You can plot levels, y/y changes, or rebased levels. You can toggle a comparison to national levels, and look at all homes, single family homes, or condos (where data is available). A friendly robot generates a summary of the trend just below the chart. Social media buttons generate a post with some pithy (editable) commentary and the chart. You can download the data. It works nicely on your phone.

posts.title: Are you a Claude Code Virgin?
posts.summary: The post asks whether readers have meaningfully used Claude Code (defined as 10+ hours with the Opus model in CLI). Sunderji argues there's a binary divide between experienced users and others, claiming only hands-on experience reveals Claude Code's genuine capabilities. He estimates spending 8 of his 12 daily work hours with Claude Code running analyses, but warns the technology's addictive nature poses an underrated risk to work-life balance.
posts.text:
Remember the scene in The 40 Year Old Virgin where Steve Carell is describing a woman’s breasts?

SC: “They were nice…you know how you grab a woman’s breast and it’s..and you feel it and…it feels like a bag of sand…when you’re touching it?”

Friend: “…have you ever felt a woman’s breast before, man?”

There’s something false when people describe things they haven’t experienced. There’s usually a tell, sometimes subtle. I tend to notice it when reading research and opinion pieces about the future of our lives with AI; there’ll be something the author writes that makes it clear they’ve never used Claude Code.

There is a chasm between those who’ve used the technology—and here I mean for a minimum of 10 hours, running the Opus model, in the CLI—and those who haven’t.

In a recent Claude Code teach-in I likened this to the gap I see between my friends who are parents vs. not. My happily married and childless Brooklyn friends recently tried to enlist my wife and me in a best-burger-in-the-city hunt during prime nap time—a delightful suggestion but only one someone without an overtired toddler would make (also, I already know what the best burger is).

Now I see a new fault line being drawn: Claude Code users vs. not. And here I am again being specific, because using ChatGPT or, god help me, Copilot, is not the same thing.

posts.title: What Does Your Grocery Store Say About Your Neighborhood?
posts.summary: The post asks whether grocery store types correlate with neighborhood wealth and home price trends. Data from 32,000+ store openings since the mid-1970s shows Trader Joe's locations outperform national home price averages by 6% within three years, while Walmart and Dollar General neighborhoods underperform by 4% and 2% respectively. Trader Joe's neighborhoods are already affluent ($425,000 median homes, 52% college-educated), suggesting the chain selects areas with existing growth potential rather than catalyzing it.
posts.text:
Home prices in ZIP codes where a Trader Joe's opens outperform the national average by 6% over the following three years. In Walmart ZIPs, they underperform by 4%. I matched more than 32,000 store openings dating back to the mid-1970s to home price data at the ZIP-code level, and layered in Census demographics for recent years. Each dot in the chart below represents a single store opening; the x-axis shows how that ZIP code's home prices performed relative to the national average in the three years after the store opened.

Rich and getting richer

Residents of neighborhoods where Trader Joe’s opens are unusually well-educated: 52% hold a bachelor’s degree, tied with Whole Foods for the highest rate of any chain and well above the national average of about a third. Median household income in those neighborhoods is $82,000—also the highest of any chain—and median home values sit at $425,000 before the store arrives. Yet in the three years after a Trader Joe’s opens, home prices in those ZIP codes still outperform the national average by 6%. These are not neighborhoods riding a wave that crests on arrival; Trader Joe’s location scouts appear to pick markets with room to keep running.

posts.title: Are NYC Teachers Overpaid?
posts.summary: The post asks whether NYC teachers are overpaid compared to teachers elsewhere. While NYC teachers earn $62,000 versus $37,000 in Jackson, Mississippi, after accounting for housing ($12,672 more annually), commute costs ($6,000), taxes ($3,100), and other living expenses, the NYC teacher is actually worse off financially. The high pay reflects the city's cost of living, not bloat.
posts.text:
A young K-12 teacher in New York City—the most expensive school district in the country—earns $62,000. A comparable teacher in Jackson, Mississippi, where teacher pay is the nation’s lowest, earns $37,000. Could salaries be a source of savings, helping to bring school costs here closer to the national average? The chart below suggests not: after housing, commute, taxes, and other cost-of-living differences, the NYC teacher is actually worse off.

The chart starts with the raw salary gap: $24,740. Housing takes the biggest bite: NYC teachers who head their own household pay $2,296 a month on average, versus $1,240 in Jackson. That $12,672 annual difference eats half the salary premium. Then there’s commute time—47 minutes each way in New York versus 18 in Jackson, an extra 195 hours a year, nearly five full work weeks, worth about $6,000 at the teacher’s own hourly wage. Add in groceries and services that run about 21% more in New York, plus $3,100 in additional state and city income taxes, and the $25,000 disappears entirely.

Conservative critics point to New York’s $38,000 per-pupil spending—91% above the national average—as evidence of bloat. Teacher pay has long been a target for conservative and libertarian think tanks. Indeed, fifty-nine percent of the DOE’s $43 billion budget is direct personnel costs: salaries and wages (38%), health insurance and fringe benefits (12%), and pension contributions (9%). posts.title: Mortgage Rates: 5.5% Really is the Magic Number
posts.summary: The post asks whether 5.5% is the "magic number" for mortgage rates to unlock home sales. Analysis of 50 years of data shows that year-over-year rate *changes* predict sales twice as well as rate *levels*—and sales respond reliably only when rates fall by at least 0.5 percentage points sustained over 6-12 months. Since current rates are around 6%, the consensus target of 5.5% happens to be correct, but because it represents that crucial 0.5-point drop, not because of the absolute level.
posts.text:
Happy Friday. People on the internet seem to really like my interactive home price map. You can play with it here—it’s entirely free. Today’s post, however, is only for paying subscribers.

Existing home sales averaged 4.1 million annualized in 2024, the weakest pace since the mid-1990s and a quarter below the 5.3 million average of 2018-2019. As the spring selling season approaches, the consensus is clear: mortgage rates need to fall to 5.5% to unlock the market. My analysis of 50 years of data says that 5.5% is indeed the magic number—but not for the reason most people think.

It is not the level of mortgage rates that predicts home sales, but the change. When I test every horizon from 1 to 36 months, the year-over-year change in rates explains half the variation in sales—double what the rate level explains. And the data says you need a move of at least half a percentage point before sales respond reliably. Rates today are around 6%. Half a point lower is, by pure coincidence, 5.5%.

The two charts above make the case. On the left, I plot the mortgage rate level against the sales level for each month since 1972. On the right, I plot the year-over-year rate change against the year-over-year sales change. The darker the hexagon, the more months fell in that bin.

posts.title: Visualizing Home Price Changes
posts.summary: The post asks how home prices have changed across U.S. ZIP codes over the past decade. Data shows median home prices have doubled nationally over 10 years, with a bubble map of 22,000 ZIP codes displaying price appreciation by color and population by dot size, revealing significant variation across regions.
posts.text:
Like the map shown below? The free interactive version lets you zoom into any ZIP code and toggle between price levels and changes (measured over horizons from 3 months to 15 years), among other features. Did I mention it’s free?

For the median American ZIP code, home prices have doubled over the past decade. The map below shows 10-year price changes across 22,000 ZIP codes. Each dot represents a ZIP code and is sized by population. Clusters of dots represent dense cities. Brighter blue means more appreciation; darker means less. I’ve labeled some of the notable underperformers.

This map is unconventional, for good reason. Conventional maps have two related problems.

The first is that geography and population are often inversely proportional—Wyoming is enormous but has fewer residents than a single Brooklyn ZIP code. A colored map gives Wyoming far more visual weight.

The second is subtler: even if you fix the geography, you can still mislead by plotting a number instead of a rate. A map of “PhDs by county” is really just a population map; New York will always dominate, even if its PhD share is unremarkable. Both problems cause the same distortion: the map draws your eye to the wrong places.

posts.title: Back to the Suburbs: Chicago Edition
posts.summary: Since the Covid-19 pandemic, Chicago's suburban and exurban home prices have soared while the urban core stagnated. The urban core rose just 18% while suburbs gained 45% and exurbs 48%—a 30-point gap, third-widest among major U.S. metros. Downtown neighborhoods like the Loop fell nearly 40%, while affluent suburbs like Glencoe surged 64%, with the suburban advantage continuing to widen.
posts.text:
Home prices have soared since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, but a rising tide has not lifted all boats: home prices in the suburbs and exurbs have risen far faster than city cores. Of the 50 largest U.S. metros, Chicago’s 30-point urban-exurban gap is the third widest in the country (after New York City and San Francisco). The map below shows the cumulative change in home prices for each ZIP code in and around Chicago since January 2020.

The urban core (within 10 miles of the Loop) rose just 18%; the Loop itself fell nearly 40%. Suburbs gained 45%. Exurbs rose 48%. Every ZIP code within a mile and a half of downtown lost value—River North (-13%), West Loop (-13%), South Loop (-13%), Streeterville (-5%). Gold Coast condos are essentially flat since January 2020.

The biggest winners were the affluent North Shore suburbs: Glencoe (+64%), Kenilworth (+62%), Winnetka (+57%), Highland Park (+53%). Further out, Aurora (+55%), Naperville (+49%), and Joliet (+47%) all outperformed the core handily.

In New York and San Francisco, the suburb premium is stable. In Chicago, it continues to rise. The gap between suburban and urban core appreciation was just 1 point in early 2021. By 2023, it was 15 points. By November 2025, 27 points—and still growing. Five years after the Covid-19 outbreak, the repricing of distance from downtown shows no signs of reverting.

posts.title: The Great Happiness Compression
posts.summary: American happiness has plummeted since the pandemic, with those reporting "very happy" dropping from 29% to 22%—the largest decline in the General Social Survey's 52-year history. Paradoxically, the biggest losses occurred among those who were happiest before: top earners fell 19 points (49% to 30%), while the already unhappy barely changed. The happiness gap between rich and poor compressed from 24 points to 10, suggesting social connection now predicts happiness more than income or education.
posts.text:
American happiness has fallen off a cliff. The General Social Survey has tracked this since 1972. Their data shows the share of Americans reporting they are "very happy" dropped from 29% before the pandemic to 22% in the most recent reading—the largest decline over any comparable span in the survey's 52-year history. The chart below shows the shift in the "very happy" distribution across the population, along with the ten demographic groups that experienced the biggest happiness declines.

The groups that lost the most happiness are the ones that had the most to begin with. The single biggest drop was among top income earners: their “very happy” share dropped 19 points, from 49% to 30%. Self-identified upper-class respondents fell 13 points. College graduates fell 12. People in excellent health, 11. People in “very happy” marriages, 10.

The bottom barely budged. People who describe their lives as “dull” went from 6% to 4% very happy. The lower class dropped 3 points. The financially dissatisfied, 3. Renters, 4. To be fair, they had less room to fall.

The result is a compression of the happiness distribution. Before the pandemic, top earners were 24 points more likely than bottom earners to report being very happy. Today, that gap has shrunk to 10. Owner happiness dropped 3x more than renter happiness. The college premium shrank from 9 points to 4.

posts.title: Don’t Blame Housing for Less Marriage
posts.summary: The post asks whether housing affordability explains declining marriage rates among young adults. Across 3,100 US counties, housing affordability changes explain only 4% of marriage decline variation, while concentration of less-educated racial minorities explains 45%. Marriage declined equally in affordable suburbs and expensive cities, suggesting housing costs aren't the primary driver.
posts.text:
In previous pieces, I’ve argued that declining homeownership among young adults is mostly a marriage problem: fewer people marrying means fewer people leaving their parents’ homes, forming their own households, and getting on the path to homeownership. But isn’t the decline in marriage itself a housing story? The data says no.

There is little connection between the places where housing became unaffordable and where marriage declined. Across 3,100 US counties, the change in home price-to-income ratio since 1980 explains just 4% of the variation in marriage decline. I tested dozens of variables. The strongest predictor of declining marriage, consistent with decades of academic research, is the concentration of less-educated racial minorities—which explains 45%.

The two maps below make this visible. Both outline the areas where marriage rates declined most (black borders). They differ in shading: the top map colors counties by their change in home price-to-income ratio since 1980; the bottom map colors them by the concentration of less-educated minorities. The outlines overlap with the bottom map (less-educated minorities), not the top (home price to income ratio).

Is there really no relationship between housing affordability and marriage? I tested the most important housing variables: renter burden, owner burden, rent-to-income change, home price levels, rent appreciation, and home price appreciation.
