posts.title: Young Home Ownership: the Decline Is Really a Delay
posts.summary: Young Americans own homes at lower rates than previous generations, not because they're rejecting homeownership but because marriage is delayed. Only 46% of 30-year-olds are married today versus 89% in 1970, but 85% eventually marry by age 50. As delayed marriages occur, homeownership rates should eventually converge toward historical levels.
posts.text:
The main reason fewer young Americans own their homes today compared to prior generations is that they’re not getting married at the same rate. Today, only 46% of 30-year-olds are married, compared to 89% at the peak in 1970. These would-be couples are instead single and often living with their parents. But the data suggests that both their marriage and homeownership rates will catch up when they’re older.

That’s because they’re not foregoing marriage entirely, they’re just getting married later in life. The chart below—which tracks the married share of the population by age bracket from 1880 to 2025—shows that by age 50, more than four in five Americans have still married. This is only 10 points below the 1980 peak.

The delay in getting married is largely involuntary—61% of women and 66% of men marry later than they originally intended, according to a longitudinal study tracking Americans to age 40. This may reflect the difficult tradeoffs between the still-strong desire for marriage (two in three high school seniors still intend to marry) and the falling costs of delaying it:

You don’t need to be married to have sex. The birth control pill severed this link. Cultural norms shifted in parallel: the share of 25-34 year-olds who view premarital sex as “not wrong at all” roughly doubled from 37% in 1972 to 77% in 2022.

posts.title: Why did Rents Soar in Miami and Stall in Austin?
posts.summary: The post asks why rents surged in some cities (Miami +53%) while stalling in others (San Francisco +13%) since 2019. Data shows work-from-home adoption is the strongest predictor: metros with high WFH shares (above 20%) saw median rents rise 32%, while low-WFH metros (under 11%) saw 43% increases. Remote workers fleeing city centers for suburbs reduces downtown rental demand, where most rental housing is concentrated.
posts.text:
Rents in Miami are 53% higher than in 2019. In San Francisco, they've risen just 13%. What explains the gap? Is it housing supply—or perhaps demand factors, like employment growth or population growth? Perhaps surprisingly, the single best explanation for exploding rents in some cities and tepid increases in others is the share of workers working from home. The chart below plots each metro's average work-from-home share against its cumulative rent change since 2019. The more people working from home, the less rents have increased.

San Francisco, Austin, and Denver have the weakest rent growth of any major metro since 2019, and all three have WFH shares above 20%. At the other end, Fresno, Virginia Beach, and Riverside all saw rents rise close to 50%, with WFH shares under 11%. Metros in the top half of WFH adoption saw median rents rise 32%; the bottom half, 43%.

This might seem counterintuitive—if more people work from home, wouldn’t the extra demand for living space push rents up? The answer is yes, it does—but not in city centers. Given the freedom to work remotely, people tend to leave downtowns for the suburbs (downtown populations in the 12 largest cities remain 8% below pre-pandemic levels).

This gives us the ‘donut ring’ effect I have documented in New York and San Francisco, where suburban and exurban home prices have outperformed urban cores by 30-plus points since 2020.

posts.title: Does Supply Explain DC’s Low Rent Growth?
posts.summary: DC rents grew 27% since 2019, 13 points below the national 39%, but supply doesn't explain the gap. Rent underperformance tracks job losses (worst in 2021 at –4 points when employment lagged 3.6 points), while the permit surge came later in 2022–2024 when rents actually outperformed nationally. Completions data confirms this: worst rent years (2020–2021) had fewest deliveries (~5,500/yr), while best years (2023–2025) had most (~7,200/yr).
posts.text:
Washington D.C. rents have grown 27% since January 2019—lower than national rents, which rose 39%. The standard explanation for the 13-point gap is that D.C. had more multifamily supply come online than other metros. But the oscillations in the city’s rent track its job market more closely than building permits. The chart below plots the gap between rent growth in D.C. versus the nation, and job growth between the two.

When COVID hit in April 2020, D.C. actually shed fewer jobs than the nation (+2 points), cushioned by the federal workforce. But the recovery was slower: by spring 2021, D.C. trailed national employment growth by 3.6 points, exactly when rents hit their worst underperformance (–4 points YoY). As the employment gap narrowed through 2022, rents flipped to outperformance. The pattern repeats with DOGE: federal workforce reductions pushed D.C. employment negative by fall 2025, and rents followed within months.

The periods when D.C. rents grew more slowly than national rents don’t line up with permits or actual housing deliveries in the city. Rents lagged the national average every year from 2019 through 2021, with the worst gap in 2021 (-4 points). But the permit surge came later: 2022 was the metro’s biggest year, with D.C.’s annual permit rate 40% above the national average. By 2024, D.C.’s annual permit rate had fallen below the national average.

posts.title: Living with Mom and Dad at 30
posts.summary: Why has homeownership among 30-year-olds dropped from 45% to 30% since 1990? The share living with parents or roommates nearly doubled from 17% to 32%. The root cause is declining marriage rates—among non-college-educated men, marriage fell from 58% to 36%—meaning fewer young adults establish independent households necessary for homeownership.
posts.text:
Why has homeownership among 30-year-olds fallen from 45% to 30% since 1990? The main reason is that the share still living with their parents or roommates has nearly doubled—from 17% to 32%—over the past 35 years. These young adults are not even in their own households, let alone looking to buy a home.

Getting into one’s own household really is the big barrier to homeownership. Once over that hump, it’s seemingly no tougher to become a homeowner than historically. Among married 30-year-olds, the homeownership rate has barely budged—63% in 1990, 60% today. Among single 30-year-olds living alone, the homeownership rate actually rose, from 25% to 29%.

It’s the surge in the proportion neither married nor single and living alone—but rather living with parents, roommates, or a romantic partner—that explains the steep decline in homeownership.

Why have so many young adults not moved into their own home? It’s not that they are in school—enrollment at 30 has actually fallen slightly. Nor are they more disabled—that has risen, but only very modestly. What changed is that far fewer are getting married.

There is a world where all these people not getting married are living alone—in their own place—rather than cohabiting. But that’s not the case. Increasingly, single 30-year-olds are living in households where their name is not on the lease or mortgage. posts.title: How I use Claude Code
posts.summary: Aziz Sunderji shares ten strategies for using Claude Code effectively for data analysis and writing. Key practices include creating a CLAUDE.md instruction file (~200 lines covering rules and guardrails), building custom slash commands for repeated workflows, maintaining memory files for persistent knowledge, and connecting external tools via Model Context Protocol. He emphasizes automating mistakes into permanent rules so Claude gradually requires shorter prompts and produces publication-ready outputs.
posts.text:
I’ve spent the last year using Claude Code for most of my work — data analysis, chart-making, research, writing drafts. Here are the top 10 things I have learned about using Claude Code effectively.

1. Write a CLAUDE.md file

Claude Code reads a file called CLAUDE.md at the start of every session. It’s your instructions file. Mine is about 200 lines — API keys, file paths, color palette, chart formatting rules, writing tone, and behavioral guardrails. Almost every line exists because Claude got something wrong and I wanted it fixed permanently.

The behavioral rules matter most. “Always use D3 for charts, never matplotlib.” “Never fabricate statistics.” “Surface anything that looks off — low match rates, dropped rows, implausible results.” Claude will silently work around problems if you let it, so I require it to list every judgment call it made.

2. Build custom slash commands

Slash commands are saved prompts that expand into full multi-step instructions. If you have a workflow you repeat, encode it once and never think about the steps again.

I have a /new-project command that creates a project folder, writes a starter script with my boilerplate, and creates a linked Notion research page. A /write-article command that gathers all the data work I’ve done in a session, surveys what other outlets have published on the topic, reads my previous articles to calibrate tone, and produces a full article draft for me to edit. A /deep-search command that tells Claude Code to do ext

posts.title: Silicon Valley is Hoarding Technical PhDs
posts.summary: The post asks where America's technical PhDs are concentrated and what this means for AI development. The Bay Area dominates with 44,000 PhDs in computer science, math, electrical engineering, and physics—nearly double New York's 23,000 and representing one in six of the nation's total. While secondary cities like Seattle and Dallas are growing faster percentage-wise, the Bay Area's concentration remains unmatched and continues expanding.
posts.text:
OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and xAI are all headquartered within 30 miles of each other in the Bay Area, drawing from a talent pool no other metro can match. As AI becomes the dominant technology of the next decade—if not the next century—the people building it are already concentrated in one place. The chart below plots where America's technical PhDs live. Each bubble is a metro area. Each bubble’s position along the horizontal axis represents the density of technical PhDs in that city. The size of the bubbles represents the number of technical PhDs in each.

The Bay Area has 44,000 working PhDs in computer science, math, electrical engineering, and physics — the four fields that account for nearly all AI research talent. That’s nearly double the next city by count (New York, 23,000) and more than double the next major metro by concentration (Boston, 44 per 10,000 adults). About one in six of the country’s technical PhDs lives in the Bay Area.

New York City is a clear underperformer here. In 2010 New York and the Bay Area had roughly the same number of technical PhDs. Since then the Bay Area has added another 25,000; New York added only about 6,000.

Many of the metros that rank highest in PhD density are university towns — Ann Arbor, Princeton, State College — where research staff and faculty, not students, drive the numbers. posts.title: The Sweatpants Dividend
posts.summary: The post asks how working from home affects happiness and time use. Workers doing jobs from home log 46 fewer minutes working, 49 fewer commuting, and 16 fewer grooming, reallocating time to sleep, TV, cooking, and childcare. Census data suggests this mix makes remote workers 20% happier overall, though this benefit remains concentrated among college graduates.
posts.text:
Half of all white collar workers now work from home at least one day a week. 16% of them work entirely from home—double the 2019 rate. Analyzing data from the Census Bureau’s American Time Use Survey, the chart below shows how a work-from-home (WFH) day differs from an office day.

Those working from home log 46 fewer minutes of work and 49 fewer of commuting, plus 16 fewer minutes of grooming. The freed-up time scatters across domestic life: 27 extra minutes of sleep, 16 of TV, 13 of cooking and eating, 12 of childcare, and 6 of exercise.

This makes workers much happier. We know this because the Census Bureau measures how happy people feel doing various activities. Unsurprisingly, people have never loved working or commuting. And now they’re replacing almost 2 hours of those activities with a mix of things they reportedly do enjoy.

Based on the change in the mix of activities and the degree of happiness associated with each, I calculate that people are 20% happier working from home. And that’s without accounting for the additional sleep (people can’t rate how happy they are sleeping).

This is almost exclusively a college-educated perk. College graduates work from home about 60% more often than those with only a high school diploma. And the gap is widening: the share of college graduates reporting any WFH rose 13 percentage points since 2019, compared to only 4 points for workers without a degree.

posts.title: We Deserve Better Billionaires
posts.summary: The post asks whether modern billionaires give enough to charity compared to their wealth. Data shows only 3 of the 17 billionaires worth $50+ billion (Buffett, Gates, Bloomberg) have given away more than 5% of their peak wealth, while 76% of all billionaires gave away less than 5%. Bezos has given $4 billion (2% of his $225 billion fortune)—less than two months of his annual wealth growth—compared to Gilded Age industrialists like Carnegie who gave away 90% of theirs.
posts.text:
One might have hoped that Jeff Bezos—net worth $225 billion—would fund the Washington Post as a philanthropic venture rather than a business one. Instead, he has cut a third of its newsroom and closed some of its foreign bureaus. But to dwell on the behavior of one billionaire is to miss the forest for the trees. The chart below ranks lifetime charitable giving as a share of peak wealth for the 17 living billionaires worth $50 billion or more alongside three Gilded Age industrialists. Bezos is hardly an outlier. Only three of the group of modern billionaires—Buffett, Gates, and Bloomberg—have given away more than 5%.

Bezos has given away roughly $4 billion over his entire lifetime—about two percent of his $225 billion fortune, according to Forbes. And since his wealth—invested at the S&P 500’s long-run average—grows by more than $22 billion a year, his lifetime giving amounts to about two months of passive appreciation. For context, this is far less than the roughly $15 billion he has poured into Blue Origin. Bezos’s largest philanthropic commitment, the $10 billion Bezos Earth Fund, has disbursed only about $2.3 billion at the halfway point of its ten-year timeline.

It is not as though Amazon stock is uniquely difficult to give away. When Bezos and MacKenzie Scott divorced in 2019, she received a quarter of their Amazon stake, then worth roughly $36 billion. posts.title: How I Use AI
posts.summary: Aziz Sunderji uses Claude Code (an AI coding agent) connected to a 23GB data lake via Model Context Protocol to automate his workflow, enabling him to publish daily articles instead of weekly while improving quality. The top AI models have increased from handling four minutes of equivalent human expert work in late 2023 to over six hours today. Success with AI depends on constantly tinkering to discover where capabilities excel versus fail.
posts.text:
If you look over my shoulder on any given workday, you’ll see two windows. On the left, a black one (Terminal) where I’m chatting with Claude Code, an AI-powered coding agent. On the right, a white one—a Notion page slowly becoming an article. This is how I use AI these days.

Beneath the surface of these two windows is a massive, interconnected system, comprised of a 23GB “data lake” (processed data, from the Census Bureau and other sources), slash commands (sets of procedures for my coding agent to run on my command), and a ream of pedantic preferences that only AI would willingly suffer (everything from font and color preferences to writing style). The terminus of this system is an article I publish on Substack—a few paragraphs of text and a single, beautiful chart.

I didn’t have this system a year ago. I was manually writing code in Python, spending hours Googling things, and constantly bugging my wife to edit my work. I was publishing once a week, at best.

These days I write an article every single day and—whatever you think of my work—I hope it’s clear that the quality has improved. It’s certainly now getting a lot more attention from people I respect. For those of you here for the charts, you’ve seen me experiment with new kinds of visualizations, like this one. I still bug my wife, but more for sport than because I need her editing help.

posts.title: Where do Parents Find the Time?
posts.summary: The post asks how working parents of young children find time for childcare, which consumes 1 hour 40 minutes per weekday. Parents sacrifice 16 fewer minutes of sleep and 24 fewer minutes of work, plus 28 minutes of screen time daily. Despite losing 16 minutes of sleep overall, parents report higher happiness (4.2/6) than non-parents (4.0/6), with sleep-deprived parents of infants reporting the highest satisfaction.
posts.text:
Americans spend more time at home than we used to, but that additional home time looks totally different for parents (especially of young children) compared to non parents. The chart below—which I compiled by analyzing the Census Bureau’s American Time Use Survey—tracks the difference in time use between working parents of small children vs working non parents. Areas above zero are activities parents do more of; areas below are what they give up.

Parents of children under six spend an hour and 40 minutes per weekday on childcare. Where do they get that time?

The morning childcare wave comes mostly from sleep: parents of young children sleep 16 fewer minutes between 4 and 9 a.m. They also do less work in the morning—which continues throughout the day (by 6 p.m. they will have done 24 fewer minutes of work).

Parents recoup the time needed for childcare in the evening from TV and other screen time: parents do 28 fewer minutes of phone/TV time between 5 and 10 p.m., redirecting nearly all of it to childcare (43 extra minutes over those five hours).

By 9 p.m., parents have accumulated a sleep deficit of 28 minutes compared to non-parents. They claw some of it back by going to bed earlier, but still end the day 16 minutes short (parents to infants end the day with 32 minutes less sleep).

posts.title: The Condo Crisis
posts.summary: Why are condos underperforming single-family homes? Since January 2020, single-family homes appreciated 46% versus 34% for condos, widening their price premium to a record 22% ($74,000 gap). The pandemic drove demand for space and remote work, but stricter lending standards post-Surfside collapse and surging insurance costs have made condos structurally more expensive to own, with condo prices now declining in most major metros.
posts.text:
Since January 2020, single-family homes in the US have appreciated 46%. Condos have only risen by 34%. The chart below shows Zillow’s Home Value Index for single-family homes and condos across 12 major metros, rebased to January 2020 = 100. Through 2019, the two property types appreciated at similar rates. Since then, single-family homes have surged ahead.

For 25 years, the price premium of single-family homes over condos typically ranged from 8 to 17%. It is now 22%, the widest on record—a $74,000 gap, up from $30,000 five years ago. In San Francisco, condos are 4% below their pre-pandemic value while single-family homes are up 24%. In New York, 8% vs. 46%. The gap was already building around 2016–2017; the pandemic supercharged it.

And the downturn is accelerating: condo prices are now declining in every top-25 metro except New York, Chicago, Boston, and a handful of Midwest/Northeast markets.

What’s driving this? Partly demand for space. Americans spend nearly an hour less per day outside the home than in 2019, and one in three employed people now work from home on any given workday, up from one in four before the pandemic. More time at home means more demand for square footage, yards, and privacy. This is consistent with my finding that suburbs are now much more highly valued relative to urban cores than they were five years ago.

But there is another factor: condos have become structurally more expensive to own, harder to finance, and harder to sell. After the Surfsid

posts.title: We Should Watch Less TV
posts.summary: The post asks why Americans aged 25-54 spend a quarter of their waking hours on TV and passive leisure—more than any activity except work—yet rate it dead last in meaningfulness (3.8/6). The data shows that meaningful activities like socializing (5.2/6), volunteering (5.2/6), and childcare (5.3/6) comprise only 12% of waking time, while TV occupies nearly twice as much despite scoring lowest in both meaning and happiness (4.3/6).
posts.text:
Americans aged 25 to 54 spend roughly a quarter of their non-sleep hours on TV and passive leisure, more time than any activity except work, yet rate it dead last in meaningfulness among daily activities. The treemap below shows how this group divides their day, according to the Census Bureau’s American Time Use Survey. Each rectangle is an activity, sized by the share of waking time it occupies, and colored by how meaningful people report finding it, from red (low meaning) to green (high meaning).

Our days are a patchwork of activities—but the things we spend the most time on are not the most meaningful. Work, the biggest share at 29% of waking activity time, scores a relatively low 4.3 out of 6. (This may not resonate with every reader here: knowledge workers tend to be more passionate about their jobs than the average.)

The most meaningful activities comprise small slivers of the day: religious practice (5.5 out of 6), childcare (5.3), volunteering (5.2), and socializing (5.2). Together these add up to only about 12% of waking time. TV occupies nearly twice as much, despite scoring dead last in meaning at 3.8 out of 6. That is below housework, below work, below every other activity the survey measures. And these are not outside assessments: the TV watchers themselves, rating the meaningfulness of what they just finished doing, place it last.

The same survey asked respondents to rate not just the degree of meaning in each activity but also their happiness while doing it.

posts.title: If California was a Country
posts.summary: California's GDP reached $4 trillion in 2024, making it the world's fourth-largest economy, up from eighth place ($1.5 trillion) in 2003. Its 4.8% annual growth outpaced European rivals like France and the UK. However, California faces a housing affordability crisis: despite high per-capita income ($103,000), unequal income distribution and soaring home prices are driving residents to other states.
posts.text:
California’s GDP reached $4 trillion in 2024, passing Japan to become the world’s fourth-largest economy. The chart below tracks the ten largest economies from 2003 to 2024. The width of each ribbon is proportional to GDP.

In 2003, California ranked eighth globally at $1.5 trillion, behind Italy, France, the United Kingdom, and China. It passed Italy in 2012, France in 2015, the UK in 2017, and Japan in 2024. California’s nominal GDP grew at 4.8% per year over that stretch, roughly double the 2–3% pace of the European economies it leapfrogged. At current growth rates, California will surpass Germany in 2031.

Texas is growing faster in absolute terms: 5.8% per year versus California’s 4.8%. But the per capita growth rates are nearly identical, 4.1% for Texas versus 4.3% for California, because Texas is absorbing people as fast as it’s adding output. California leads $103,000 to $89,000 in nominal GDP per capita. At the current differential, Texas wouldn’t surpass California until 2041.

There is a dark side to California’s success. Home prices are strongly correlated with incomes. California has some of the highest home prices in the country. This isn’t a problem in itself. It becomes problematic because incomes—and therefore access to housing—are unequally distributed. A rising number of Californians are moving to other states because they cannot afford the quality and quantity of housing they want in their home state.

posts.title: Sunderji's Paradox
posts.summary: Sunderji's Paradox asks why the median renter's share of income spent on housing hasn't fallen despite real incomes rising across all deciles since 2005—today's median renter ($50,000) earns more than the top 20% in 2005 yet still spends 32% on rent. The data shows this pattern persists globally and historically: from 1868 Berlin to modern Australia, renters consistently spend 25–33% of income on housing, while other necessities' shares have declined dramatically (clothing fell from 20% to 3% since 1948). Housing costs rise with incomes because everyone bids with more money for fixed-supply locations.
posts.text:
I usually paywall Friday posts, but this article is for everyone. Please consider supporting my work for $8/month.

Easterlin’s paradox: the rich are happier than the poor, but as countries get richer, they don’t get happier. I want to propose an analogous paradox for housing—Sunderji’s paradox: the rich spend a smaller share of their income on rent than the poor, but as countries have grown richer, the median share of income going to housing hasn’t fallen.

The chart below plots the share of income spent on rent across income deciles, from 2005 to 2024. Real incomes have increased for every single decile. Consider the median renter, who today earns $50,000—they would have been in the top 20% of renters in 2005. Yet today they still spend the same 32% of their income on rent as they did in 2005. What’s going on?

The cross-sectional gradient shown in the chart—where higher earners pay a smaller share—has been documented for over 150 years. Economists call it Schwabe’s Law, after Hermann Schwabe, head of the Berlin Statistical Bureau, who published research in 1868 showing that as family income rose, the rent share fell—but the “middle” consistently hovered around 25%.

The same pattern appears across time and geography. Charles Booth’s 1880s surveys of London’s East End found laborers paying 25–33% of income for even the most squalid housing. posts.title: The Sun Belt goes Vertical
posts.summary:
# Summary

Are Sun Belt cities densifying as rapidly as coastal cities? While Dallas, Houston, Atlanta, Miami, and Phoenix each added over 100,000 apartment units since 2010—with Dallas and Houston roughly doubling their stock—Sun Belt metros added only 104 large-building units per 1,000 new residents versus 180 for coastal cities. Despite this record construction, large apartments comprised just 11% of Sun Belt housing by 2024, still below coastal cities' 2010 baseline of 13%.
posts.text:
I showed yesterday that Atlanta has hit the limits of sprawl and is densifying from the inside out. That pattern extends across the Sun Belt. Between 2010 and 2024, Dallas, Houston, Atlanta, Miami, and Phoenix each added more than 100,000 residential units in large apartment buildings. The map below shows this: each bar is a metro area; blue represents the stock of large-building units that existed in 2010, yellow is what has been added since. Cities are labeled by their rank in multifamily growth. New York is capped for legibility.

Dallas and Houston are the standouts — both roughly doubled their stock of large-building units since 2010. Austin, Charlotte, and San Antonio grew even faster in percentage terms.

But adjust for population growth and the picture changes. For every 1,000 new residents in a Sun Belt metro, just 104 units were added in large apartment buildings. Coastal cities added 180. Seattle added half as many people as Dallas but built 187 large-building units per 1,000 new residents — 59% more than Dallas’s 118. Atlanta added 106. Charlotte, the fastest-growing large metro in the country, added just 59.

In 2010, just 7% of housing in the median Sun Belt metro sat in buildings with 20 or more units. By 2024 that share had climbed to 11%. But coastal cities were already at 13% in 2010, and reached 17% by 2024. After 14 years of record multifamily construction, the Sun Belt still sits below where coastal cities started.

posts.title: The Millennial Homeownership Problem Is Mostly a Marriage Problem
posts.summary: Why do fewer Millennials own homes than Boomers? The data shows that at age 30, only 33% of Millennials owned homes versus 50% of Boomers, primarily because Millennials marry later and less frequently—just 42% are married household heads compared to 63% of Boomers. When comparing married couples directly, the homeownership gap shrinks to 8 points, suggesting the problem is delayed marriage rather than reduced ability to buy homes.
posts.text:
At age 30, only a third of Millennials owned their home, compared to almost half of Boomers at that age. By age 40, the difference is smaller but remains. What’s the explanation? The charts below plot the journey from birth to marriage and homeownership, snapshotting living arrangements for the two generations at ages 30, 35, and 40.

The headline homeownership gap exists because Boomers married at higher rates—and earlier—than Millennials, and because the rate of homeownership is higher for married household heads than for those living at home (0% ownership rate) or for single people. At 30, almost one in three Millennials still live with parents or friends, versus only 17% of Boomers. And at that age only 42% of Millennials are married household heads, compared with 63% of Boomers.

If we compare apples to apples—and look at Millennials later in life—the gap nearly vanishes. Of married Millennials who head their own households, 59% own at age 30, versus 67% for an equivalent Boomer—an 8-point gap that shrinks to a mere 5 points by 40. And among single heads, the gap is essentially zero: at 30, single Millennial heads were actually slightly more likely to own (29% vs 28%).

Millennials are leaving home and getting married as they age, but later and less than Boomers. This is likely due to both shifting preferences and the constraints of affordability. posts.title: Atlanta City Limits
posts.summary: Atlanta's housing growth has slowed dramatically from 4.8% in the 1970s to 1.1% in the 2010s and 0.6% in 2020-23. The post examines why, proposing that Sunbelt cities like Atlanta have exhausted buildable land within their 45-minute commute zones, where 70% of the metro's 2.5 million housing units sit. As a result, growth is now occurring through downtown densification rather than outward sprawl.
posts.text:
Atlanta’s housing stock grew by 4.8% in the 1970s, but by the 2010s, that rate had fallen to 1.1%. It was just 0.6% in 2020-23. We see the same slowdown across Sunbelt cities, including Phoenix, Dallas, and Miami. Why?

The map below holds part of the answer. It’s a dot-density map of housing in and around the Atlanta metro. Each dot represents 20 housing units. Green dots are pre-2010 housing; yellow dots are units built since 2010. The black dotted boundary marks a 45-minute drive from downtown (roughly an hour at rush hour).

Dense housing fills the commuter envelope, then drops off sharply at the edge. The Atlanta metro has 2.5 million housing units, 388,000 of them built since 2010. Seventy percent of all housing sits within the 45-minute boundary.

Cities like Atlanta grew by sprawling outward. But they’ve largely exhausted the land within commuting distance of their job centers. Most people don’t want to drive more than 45 minutes to get to work. As I’ve written previously, Atlanta car commuters already face the second-longest commute nationally.

Having hit this boundary, you can see how the city is growing in recent years: it’s densifying. The highest concentration of yellow dots in the map, representing post 2010 construction, is urban infill in the downtown core.

If this explanation—a geographic limit to city expansion—seems obvious, you should know it is the minority view. The consensus view ascribes the slowdown in growth to regulation.

posts.title: Home Prices Five Years After Covid
posts.summary: Since January 2020, US metro home prices surged in 2021-22, then fell during the 2023 rate hikes, and have been flat or slightly negative since. Unlike the 2007-09 cycle, metros that rose most didn't fall most—Charlotte and Miami held gains despite recent declines, while Florida's 2025 weakness hasn't erased pandemic-era gains.
posts.text:
ICYMI: Last Friday—for paying subscribers—I published a visual analysis about how AI company stock options are fueling a rebound in Silicon Valley’s housing market. Upgrade to read it here.

The pandemic reshaped the housing market: new migration patterns, near-zero interest rates, and a surge in transactions. Prices shifted dramatically: first up, then down. Where does this leave home prices in major US metros? The heatmap below plots year-over-year price changes across major metros since January 2020, with cumulative appreciation labeled on the right side. Three patterns stand out.

Synchronicity

Though real estate is local, macro forces move home prices in lockstep more than people think. Almost all metros surged in 2021-22, fell amid high mortgage rates in 2023, and have been flat or slightly negative since.

It’s not just boom and bust

In the 2007-09 cycle, the metros that rose the most subsequently fell the most. That pattern doesn’t hold this time. Charlotte and Miami rallied hard but didn’t give much back. Minneapolis never rose nor fell much. Migration, local industry health, supply constraints, and rising insurance premiums all shaped outcomes differently across markets.

Florida’s weakness hasn’t overshadowed its strength

One of the big stories of 2025 was falling Florida home prices, driven by surging insurance costs, return-to-office shifts, and departing Canadian snowbirds. But Miami and Tampa rallied so hard during the pandemic that even after tumbling throu

posts.title: Population Growth Slows to a Crawl
posts.summary:
# Summary

The post examines why U.S. population growth slowed to just 1.8 million (July 2024-2025), with only 519,000 from natural increase and 1.26 million from immigration. Key findings: natural increase collapsed from 923,000 in 2019 to ~500,000; international migration fell 54% year-over-year to 1.3 million; and domestic migration southward slowed significantly, with North Carolina leading at 84,000 versus Florida's 311,000 in 2022.
posts.text:
According to Census Bureau data released this week, the United States added a mere 1.8 million people between July 2024 and July 2025. The maps below decompose each state's population change into its three components—natural change (births minus deaths), net domestic migration, and net international migration—as a percentage of each state’s population.

Of the 1.8mn rise in population, only 519,000 came from natural increase (births minus deaths). The remaining 1.26 million came from international migration. Five states lost population: California (-9,500), Vermont (-1,900), Hawaii (-2,100), West Virginia (-1,300), and New Mexico (-1,300). New York grew by just 1,008 people.

Three themes stood out to me:

1. Natural increase has collapsed. In 2019 births exceeded deaths by 923,000. This crashed to 146,000 in 2021, and has recovered only to roughly 500,000, where it has sat for three years. Before the pandemic, deaths exceeded births in just 5 states. At the COVID peak, 27. In 2025: 18, still far above the pre-pandemic norm. West Virginia has the worst natural change rate in the country, driven by high mortality. Maine and Vermont are next, due to low birth rates.

2. International migration fell 54% year-over-year, from 2.7 million to 1.3 million—much slower, but still double the 2019 rate. Florida (+179,000), Texas (+167,000), and California (+109,000) received the most. As a share of population, the fastest growing were Florida (0.76%), Washington (0.58%), and DC (0.57%).

posts.title: What Explains Low Millennial Home Ownership?
posts.summary: Why do fewer Millennials own homes than Boomers? Two key differences explain the 18-point ownership gap (43% vs. 25%): 31% of Millennials live with parents or roommates at age 30 versus 19% of Boomers, and only 61% of Millennials are married by 30 compared to 77% of Boomers. Among married household heads, the ownership gap narrows to just 8 points.
posts.text:
Why do so few Millennials own their home compared with prior generations? The diagram below traces the path from birth to living arrangement at age 30 for Millennials and Boomers. It reveals two junctures where the generations diverged.

First, household formation: 31% of Millennials at age 30 still live with parents or roommates, compared to just 19% of Boomers at the same age—a 12-percentage-point gap that immediately disqualifies Millennials from the ownership track.

Second, marriage: among those who do form households, only 61% of Millennials are married by age 30, versus 77% of Boomers.

These two factors—not leaving the nest and not marrying, at least by age 30—account for the bulk of the 18-point ownership gap (43% for Boomers vs. 25% for Millennials). Part of this comes down to shifting preferences and values, but stretched affordability is also an important driver.

Strikingly, conditional on being a married household head, ownership rates are much closer: 68% of married Boomer heads owned at 30, compared to 60% of Millennials—an 8-point gap, far smaller than the headline 18-point difference.

charts.context: Why do so few Millennials own their home compared with prior generations? The diagram below traces the path from birth to living arrangement at age 30 for Millennials and Boomers. It reveals two junctures where the generations diverged.

posts.title: Is this a Weird Housing Market?
posts.summary: Does the US housing market show unusual regional divergence? Ridge plot data from 2001-present reveals this isn't abnormal dispersion—ZIP code price change spread is below average. Instead, the oddity is the average price change hovering near zero, versus the typical +5% annual gain.
posts.text:
I recently received a call from a reporter looking for my views on what he felt was a very odd US housing market. “Florida is cratering but New York is booming—this is not normal,” he said. It got me thinking—is this really an atypical market? Are different parts of the country moving in different directions, and more drastically than usual?

My investigation led me to make the “ridge plot” below: it shows the distribution of home price changes (measured year-over-year) by ZIP code at the end of every year, going back to 2001. The taller the ridge at any point, the more ZIP codes fall into that price change bucket.

My conclusion is that this is indeed an abnormal housing market, but not in the way the journalist suggested. It’s not that home prices are rising a lot in some places and falling a lot in others—the spread (standard deviation) of price changes across ZIP codes is actually below average.

Instead, what’s weird about this market is that the average price change today sits so close to zero (in a typical year the average is close to +5%). A normal distribution of price changes is straddling this average—producing a mix of risers and fallers even without unusually high dispersion.

posts.title: Back to the Suburbs: Bay Area Edition
posts.summary: Since January 2020, San Francisco's urban core fell 7.5% while suburbs gained 24% and exurbs rose 30%, creating a 37-point gap—the second-widest among major U.S. metros. Downtown neighborhoods like SoMa dropped 25%, while exurban areas like San Ramon surged 54%. Despite office recalls, the suburban preference appears permanent.
posts.text:
Home prices have soared since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, but a rising tide has not lifted all boats: home prices in the suburbs and exurbs have risen far faster than city cores. Of the 50 largest U.S. metros, San Francisco’s 37-point urban-exurban gap is the second widest in the country (second only to New York City). The map below shows the cumulative change in home prices for each ZIP code in and around San Francisco since January 2020.

The urban core (within 10 miles of downtown) fell 7.5%; downtown San Francisco proper fell even more, with SoMa down 25% and the Tenderloin down 23%. By contrast, suburbs gained 24% on average. Exurbs rose 30%. The biggest winners were places like San Ramon (+54%) and Danville (+49%) along the I-680 corridor—and coastal retreats like Stinson Beach (+46%).

We are now 5 years out from the Covid-19 outbreak. All the workers who were going to be called back to the office have been called back. Yet, the exurb premium is stable. It looks to me like the greater value San Franciscans place on suburban living is here to stay.

posts.title: The Price of Endless Summer
posts.summary: California lost 254,000 residents to other states in 2024, double the 2010-2019 average. Key destinations were Nevada, Texas, Arizona, and Florida, with Florida seeing a 13-fold increase in net migration from California. Critically, departing residents are increasingly affluent and college-educated, citing housing costs as their primary reason for leaving—even high-income households ($150K+) now prioritize cheaper housing over employment opportunities.
posts.text:
California lost 254,000 residents to other states in 2024 on a net basis—double the 2010-2019 average of 125,000. Who’s leaving, why, and where are they going?

The top destinations were Nevada (32K net), Texas (32K), Arizona (24K), and Florida (20K). But the composition of this outflow is shifting.

The biggest change is in flows to Florida. California’s net loss to Florida has grown from just 1,500 annually in 2010-2019 to over 20,000 in 2024—a 13-fold increase. Tennessee (+431%) and Nevada (+66%) also saw large gains. Meanwhile, Oregon actually saw a decline (-24%).

The characteristics of leavers has also evolved. High-income households ($150K+) now make up 23% of departing household heads, up from 12.5% in 2011-2019. Young college graduates (25-44 with BA+) are also a larger share. Meanwhile, lower-income households without college degrees fell from 41% to 31% of the outflow. The exodus is becoming more affluent and educated.

The reasons for leaving are shifting too. Between 2011-2019 and 2021-2024, employment-related moves dropped from 48% to 33% of California departures, while housing cost concern-driven moves rose from 22% to 31%.

Strikingly, high-income households ($150K+) are now more likely to cite “cheaper housing” than low-income households as their reason for leaving. Among high earners, this reason nearly tripled from 7% in 2011-2019 to 20% in 2021-2024.

posts.title: Around Zero, Noise Looks like Signal
posts.summary: The post asks why home prices are rising in some regions and falling in others, unusually divergent. Data shows 63% of ZIP codes (16,500) saw price gains while 37% (9,800) saw declines, concentrated in the Midwest/Northeast versus Sunbelt losses. This geographic split merely reflects national appreciation near 0%—statistical noise around the mean—though Sunbelt weakness stems from reversed migration and oversupply.
posts.text:
At the end of 2025, home prices had risen from a year earlier in 16,500 ZIP codes (63%). Prices were lower than a year earlier in 9,800 ZIP codes. Gains were concentrated in the Midwest and Northeast—with over 85% of ZIP codes in states like Wisconsin, Indiana, Connecticut, and Illinois seeing appreciation. Losses were predominant in the Sunbelt, where Florida (96% of ZIPs), Texas (75%), Arizona (73%), and California (78%) saw widespread price drops.

It’s unusual to see home prices rising in one part of the country and falling elsewhere. Even if ‘real estate is local’, macro factors—interest rates, employment growth, etc.—tend to dominate, pushing most ZIP codes in the same direction, even if by different degrees.

So the divergence we see today—with some ZIPs up and some down—is surprising. But it merely reflects a statistical quirk: with national appreciation hovering near 0%, a normal distribution around that threshold yields a mix of gainers and losers.

As for the geographic pattern apparent in the map, the black swathes across the Sunbelt (representing falling prices) reflect a supply/demand imbalance: pandemic-era migration flows to the area reversed just as a lot of new construction came online.

If the housing market heats back up, this apparent divide will quietly disappear—even in Sunbelt ZIPs remain the laggards, the distribution will shift to the right, and nearly all ZIPs will be in the blue again.

posts.title: Homeownership Looks Worse When You Measure it Properly
posts.summary: The post asks why homeownership appears lower for younger generations. Using per capita ownership rates (owners as share of all adults) instead of household heads reveals the true problem: only 48% of 35-year-old Millennials own homes versus 57% of Boomers, partly because many live with family or friends rather than forming independent households. Gen Z is following the same trajectory as Millennials.
posts.text:
Most charts showing homeownership by generation understate the problem for Millennials and Gen Z. The standard measure—owners as a share of household heads—misses everyone who hasn’t formed their own household yet. And these days, that’s a lot of young people. This chart uses a more revealing metric: the per capita ownership rate (owners as a share of all adults in each generation).

A big part of the reason that only 48% of Millennials own their home at 35 years of age (Boomers: 57%) is that many are simply not striking out on their own and forming households (they’re living with friends or parents). There is a silver lining though: for the first time, young people are doing no worse than their immediate predecessors: Gen Zs are tracing the same arc as Millennials.

posts.text:

posts.title: Why do People Leave New York City?
posts.summary: New York City's population declined for a decade before recently rebounding, likely to reverse again. Census data reveals 82% of emigrants stay nearby (Long Island, Westchester), citing housing as the primary reason, while the smaller group moving interstate are highly educated and leave mainly for jobs. Housing policy could stem local outmigration, but interstate departures reflect job opportunities elsewhere that NYC cannot easily counter.
posts.text:
In the most recent two years, New York City's population has been growing. But this follows a decade of declining population. In our view, it's more likely than not that—once post-pandemic migration patterns and surging international arrivals settle down—the city begins to shrink again.

On the eve of a new mayor taking office, Home Economics has been writing about whether public policy can stem these outflows.

In part one of this series we identified the source of declining population (net domestic outflows exceeding net international inflows) and found that those who are leaving the city are younger, better educated, and have higher incomes and fewer children than those who stay.

That said, the characteristics of leavers varies substantially by destination. posts.summary: Can New York City reverse decades of population decline and return to growth? The data shows NYC's population contracted over 3% from April 2020 to July 2024—twice faster than Philadelphia—driven by domestic outflows outpacing international immigration. While recent asylum seeker arrivals temporarily reversed the decline, those flows are collapsing, leaving uncertain prospects unless the city can stem departures of young, educated workers earning 13% above average.
posts.text:
New York City is having a moment.

COVID migrants are returning, plutocrats who decamped to Miami are slinking back, and the city's firms are hiring. A Muslim socialist mayor is about to take office but—despite the panic among Upper East Side moms—there are no signs of imminent Sharia law, nor is there any evidence of a tax-avoidance flight from the five boroughs. In fact, contrary to national trends, New York City rents and prices are rising healthily.

Home Economics is proudly based in midtown Manhattan. We feel this is a great place to do business. But even we have to admit that, when we look beyond the current moment, the data is worrying.

New York City's population has stagnated since the 1970s, but outright declined through the 2010s. The city's population has historically been a balance between natural growth((births minus deaths)) and international inflows offsetting domestic outflows. In recent years outflows have dominated. Looking through the recent wobbles (both down and up) to the longer term trends, New York appears to be shrinking at the fastest pace since the 1970s.

Components of change

To be fair, New York isn't alone among cities losing population.

Five of the country's ten largest cities have shrunk since the Covid pandemic began. But the pace of New York's contraction—more than 3% between April 2020 and July 2024—is twice that of the next-fastest-shrinking city, Philadelphia. posts.title: The Housing Hangover has Cleared
posts.summary: The post asks why the housing market has felt soft despite stable prices, arguing that low transaction volumes—not price drops—tell the real story. Data shows volumes surged during the pandemic (2020-22) but collapsed after mortgage rates rose in 2022; however, 85% of that excess activity has now cleared, with recent green shoots suggesting demand is returning to normal levels.
posts.text:
Few would argue that the housing market has been anything but soft over the past few years. But what does 'soft' mean? You'd be hard pressed to make the case that home prices are sufficient evidence: prices have not dropped year-over-year at the national level, though they skirted 0% in the summer of 2023 and again in the latest readings.

Instead, it's the combination of slower home price growth and few of them actually trading hands that really encapsulates the sluggishness that most housing participants, from agents to developers, are feeling. In other words, transaction volumes tell the story.

The chart below shows US housing (all home types) transaction volumes over the past 15 years((Zillow data)). Volumes surged during the pandemic, with both prices and sales soaring, but have been sluggish since mortgage rates rose in 2022.

Transaction Volumes

Part of the reason volumes have been so low is that there was a surge of activity during the pandemic. With record low mortgage rates, new-found work mobility, and the need for more domestic space, millions of people changed their living situation in 2020-22.

And anyone who had been contemplating buying over the ensuing years surely also jumped the gun, bringing forward their transaction. It's hardly surprising that we've had a fallow period—a housing hangover—after the frenzy.

The good news is that 85% of the excess activity from 2020-22 has now been swallowed by the last few years of market quietude. If activity is now sh

posts.title: The Politics of Housing: Rent Freezes and the 50-year Mortgage
posts.summary: Housing affordability has been a persistent political issue since at least 1836, but it's now increasingly polarizing along tenure lines: renters lean decisively left while homeowners lean right, with a 14-point ideological split that has intensified over time. Recent political figures exemplify this divide—NYC Mayor Mamdani champions renters while Trump proposes 50-year mortgages for homebuyers. However, the post argues that underlying income inequality, not housing supply or financing terms, is the root cause of affordability problems.
posts.text:
A month ago, New Yorkers received a booklet in the mail profiling candidates running for various municipal offices. Each profile listed the candidate's top three priorities. Leafing through the book, Home Economics noted that every single profile included housing affordability((Or at least affordability, generally)) as a first or second priority. Not one profile omitted the issue.

Housing affordability—like jobs—is a perennial concern. Newspaper archives spanning decades—even centuries—chronicle the struggles of all but the very rich in securing safe, clean, well-located housing within their budgets.

Our favorite evidence of this timelessness comes from Australian economist Cameron Murray, who cites Charles Darwin describing conditions in Sydney in January 1836:

"The number of large houses just finished and others building is truly surprising; nevertheless every one complains of the high rents and difficulty in procuring a house."

Modest Evolution Since 1836

But if housing affordability is as old as housing itself, what's new is how it's intersecting with our increasingly polarized politics.

Consider: Zoran Mamdani won the New York City mayorship largely on clever messaging around the plight of renters. posts.title: Monitoring Employment for Home Price Cues
posts.summary: Employment growth strongly predicts home price appreciation within major U.S. cities, with top-tier employment growth cities outperforming bottom-tier by 6+ percentage points nearly 90% of the time since 2002. Recent data shows Charlotte leading at +2.5% year-over-year growth, while San Francisco (-0.5%) is the only major metro declining, reflecting tech sector weakness and remote work trends.
posts.text:
Income growth is among the strongest and most consistent predictors of home price appreciation. That’s why studies aiming to isolate the effects of other factors, such as housing supply constraints, typically control for income before assessing the impact of other factors((See this recent paper)). In short, any credible model of housing prices must account for income growth.

But incomes are hard to measure at a geographically granular level and at high frequency. Instead, we think investors should focus on employment—a useful proxy for the "wage bill" (the number of people employed x the hours they work x the wage they earn).

The Bureau of Labor Statistics provides state and MSA-level employment data every month through its Current Employment Statistic (CES) program((Here)), and at the county level through Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS)((Here)).

Employment growth correlates with home price growth

Figure 1 below shows that, within the largest 30 American cities, the top tier cities for employment growth have experienced more rapid appreciation than the bottom tier almost 90% of the time since 2002. The gap between the two has averaged over 6 percentage points.

posts.title: Geographic Diversity isn't a Policy Failure
posts.summary: Does New York's loss of financial workers signal policy failure? Data shows New York, Chicago, Baltimore, Washington, and San Francisco all slowed worker growth from 2015-25 compared to 2005-15, while Sunbelt cities like Phoenix, Dallas, and Orlando accelerated. The post argues high costs stem from productivity and agglomeration rather than policy, and geographic diversification reflects remote work enabling workers to relocate—a natural, not negative, development.
posts.text:
An article in this week's Economist Magazine argues that New York is losing its share of financial workers—a sign, they argue, that the city has lost its way, becoming entangled in bureaucracy, high taxes, and overregulation, which has pushed businesses and the wealthy to other cities.

In our view, The Economist is only partially correct about what's happening (New York losing finance jobs), and mostly incorrect about the cause.

First, it's not just New York—the trend is much broader. Consider figure 1 below, where we compare the pace of labor force growth in major cities between two decade-long periods: 2005-15 and 2015-25.

In the latter period, New York grew more slowly, but so did many other historic—and historically expensive—cities: Chicago, Baltimore, Washington, and San Francisco all added workers at a slower pace. Meanwhile, Sunbelt cities like Phoenix, Dallas, and Orlando accelerated.

Change in worker growth

Second, as the map shows, it's not just about finance. Across all industries, New York added workers at a much slower pace in the decade to 2025 than in the prior one.

Third, The Economist pins high costs in New York entirely in the policy realm: "its fealty to public unions, overregulation, a costly and expensive bureaucracy, and expensive litigation"—but none of these are the main cause of the city's high costs.

In fact, the main cause isn't nearly as sinister: it's that the city is very productive. Agglomerations of highly productive firms and workers n

posts.title: Identifying Undervalued ZIPs
posts.summary: The post asks which ZIP codes are undervalued based on home prices relative to local incomes. Using Zillow data and Census income figures across 30 major U.S. metros, it identifies ZIPs where three-bedroom home prices fall more than 30% below the price-income trend line as potentially undervalued, while those 30% above appear overvalued. The analysis uses an interactive map tool allowing users to visualize these deviations by city.
posts.text:
Home prices track incomes

The strongest and most consistent predictor of home prices is local incomes. Where incomes are high, so are prices—and when incomes rise in a given area, home prices usually follow.

This is because higher-income households have a greater ability and willingness to pay for desirable locations—those with good schools, safety, and short commutes. The sorting of geographies into high amenity / high income / high price, versus low amenity / low income / low price, operates both across cities (see chart inset) and within them. There is an extensive body of research corroborating and explaining this observation((A broad empirical literature confirms that local incomes are the dominant long-run determinant of housing prices, and that deviations from this relationship can signal over- or undervaluation. Gallin (2003) first showed that U.S. metro-level house prices and incomes are cointegrated over time, establishing income as a fundamental anchor. Li (2014) demonstrated that both labor income and wealth drive city-level price variation, reinforcing the income side of valuation models. Oikarinen et al. (2023) extended this analysis to 70 metros, finding that while house prices remain strongly correlated with incomes across cities, the slope and intercept of that relationship shift with supply elasticity and amenity growth—implying that current price-income residuals capture relative valuation rather than a stationary equilibrium. posts.title: How Would A Recession Cascade through Real Estate?
posts.summary: The post asks which real estate sectors decline first during recessions and whether they're declining now. Analysis of 2008 data shows roofing contractors, mortgage brokers, and real estate agents led downturns by 20-23 months. Today, credit intermediation and real estate agents have turned down sharply, suggesting the entire real estate sector faces recession risk despite downstream sectors like architecture still showing strength.
posts.text:
The economic outlook is especially precarious. Employment in some of the most predictive leading sectors—like credit intermediation and real estate agents—have turned down sharply. The entire real estate complex is at risk, even if those further downwind—like property managers, providers of building services, and architects—are not yet feeling the chill.

Job creation has come to a standstill. The unemployment rate, especially for recent graduates, is rising.

Will this turn into a full-blown recession? Answering that question is especially challenging these days, for two reasons.

First, the typical signals we would use to gauge the likelihood of a downturn are muddier than usual because of lingering pandemic distortions (volatile business formation and immigration, for example).

Second, some critical economic data is being delayed because of the government shutdown. Reading between the lines from the economic data that has not been affected by the shutdown, like ADP payrolls (a private sector alternate measure to nonfarm payrolls)—the picture is fairly grim.

Given these risks, smart housing market participants are spending more time looking in more detail at employment statistics (even if they are delayed). After all, the labor market provides some of the earliest and most reliable indicators of impending economic weakness.

posts.title: Introducing JobsWatch
posts.summary: Sunderji introduces JobsWatch, a tool that tracks granular employment data across nearly 90 years to monitor specific real estate sectors. Recent data shows overall construction employment is now contracting, with specialty trade contractors—particularly residential and foundation/exterior contractors—driving the decline, despite construction previously outperforming other sectors.
posts.text:
The economy is slowing. We can see it in the data: leading indicators like factory new orders, stock prices, credit spreads, and consumer expectations are all weakening.

But the economy is not a monolith. Some sectors can thrive even amid a broader slowdown. Consider what happened in 2015: an ‘industrial recession’, where [sector]Manufacturing[/sector] contracted but the rest of the economy continued to grow.

Could real estate escape this slowdown unscathed? What signals should we be watching?

The best way to monitor the health of specific real estate sectors—like architecture, remodeling, office construction, or single family rentals—is to watch employment data.

Shrinking payrolls is one of the most reliable indicators of weakening economic conditions, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases payroll data for even the smallest, most niche sectors. And since employment figures are released monthly (for the prior month), it’s some of the most timely data around.

This data is extremely useful for housing market professionals. For example, a developer planning a mixed-use project needs to know if demand from office tenants is softening. posts.title: Our National 5 Year Home Price Forecast
posts.summary: Home Economics forecasts only 1.6% national home price appreciation in 2026 and just 8.9% cumulative growth over 2025-2029, significantly below the panel consensus of 19.5%. These projections fall in the 15th and 13th percentiles of historical outcomes respectively, reflecting current home prices at 1.58 standard deviations above income-adjusted norms and elevated inventory suggesting a prolonged below-trend correction ahead.
posts.text:
Executive Summary

Home Economics projects national home price appreciation of 1.6% in 2026, placing our forecast in the 15th percentile of historical outcomes and 31st percentile relative to panel economists.

Over the full five-year forecast horizon (2025-2029), we expect cumulative appreciation of just 8.9%—a figure that falls in the 13th percentile of all historical five-year periods since 1975 and dramatically below the panel consensus of approximately 20%((When last measured, 3 months ago)). This represents less than half the historical norm, suggesting a prolonged period of below-trend growth reminiscent of the early 1990s housing correction.

This forecast emerges from a rigorous econometric model that emphasizes fundamental valuation metrics, housing supply dynamics, and momentum factors. Current conditions—with home prices sitting 1.58 standard deviations above their income-adjusted norm and new home inventory levels elevated at 9.2 months—suggest a multi-year correction lies ahead, even as the Federal Reserve embarks on an aggressive easing cycle.

Our Forecast vs History

Backdrop

Home Economics was invited to submit projections to the Pulsenomics Home Price Expectations Survey, the premier panel forecast for U.S. residential real estate. posts.title: Searching for Coastal Bargains
posts.summary: The post asks what it costs to buy coastal real estate in America. Data from 4,400 coastal zip codes shows extreme disparities: the cheapest is Corpus Christi, Texas at $78,200, while the most expensive is Atherton, California at $7.7 million—nearly 98 times higher. However, bargain coastal properties face hidden costs like soaring insurance premiums (averaging $11,836 annually in Cape Coral, Florida) that could erase $1.4 trillion in real estate value.
posts.text:
As we sit in mid-August and millions of Americans find themselves lounging on coastal beaches, many of them may be thinking: "What would it cost to have a permanent foothold here?"

Whether driven by practical retirement planning or pure voyeuristic curiosity about the ultra-wealthy's seaside compounds, we've mapped out the entire spectrum of American coastal real estate—from the surprisingly affordable to the astronomically expensive.

The Bargain Beaches

Our analysis of over 4,400 coastal zip codes shows that oceanside living doesn't always require a trust fund.

The cheapest coastal zip code in America is 78405 in Corpus Christi, Texas, where the median home price sits at just $78,200—less than many luxury SUVs. In fact, the entire Texas Gulf Coast dominates the affordability rankings, with eight of the ten cheapest coastal markets clustered around Corpus Christi.

Moving east along the Gulf, Mobile, Alabama emerges as another affordability haven. Zip codes like 36605 offer coastal proximity with median prices around $88,700.

The Atlantic Coast offers its own budget-friendly surprises. Gresham, South Carolina (29546), sitting roughly 24 miles from the ocean, provides small-town coastal access for around $91,600. Similarly, parts of coastal Alabama like Bayou La Batre (36509) offer Gulf access for under $92,000.

posts.title: Credit Drove 125 Year of Homeownership Gains
posts.summary: The post asks how American homeownership rose from 47% in 1900 to 69% in 2004, then fell to 65% today. Data from 100+ million household records shows major gains came from financial engineering—easier mortgages and down payments—not more housing. The GI Bill and Federal Housing Administration drove an 11.5 percentage point jump from 1940-1950, while the 2008 crisis revealed the dangers of loosening credit standards too far.
posts.text:
Using over 100 million household records from census microdata and quarterly housing surveys, we trace American homeownership from 47% in 1900 to its peak of 69% in 2004, and back down to 65% today. The major jumps in homeownership have come not from building more homes, but from financial engineering—making mortgages cheaper and more accessible to marginal borrowers.

The Pre-Depression Era (1900-1929)

Homeownership hovered between 46% and 48% for three decades. Buying required 30-50% down payments and short-term balloon mortgages—typically five to seven years—that limited access to the wealthy.

The Great Depression and New Deal Revolution (1930-1945)

By 1933, over 1,000 foreclosures occurred daily. Half of all mortgages fell into default. Homeownership hit 43.5% by 1940, the lowest level in our data.

The Federal Housing Administration (1934) revolutionized mortgage finance: 30-year terms replaced balloon loans, down payments dropped to 10%, and federal insurance backed qualifying mortgages. The system worked by subsidizing demand—making mortgages accessible to marginal borrowers—rather than increasing housing supply.

The Post-War Homeownership Explosion (1945-1970)

The GI Bill (1944) offered veterans zero-down mortgages at below-market rates. By 1955, it had issued 4.3 million loans totaling $33 billion.

The numbers are striking: homeownership surged from 43.5% in 1940 to 55.0% in 1950—an 11.5 percentage point jump in a single decade. It reached 61.9% by 1960 and 62.

posts.title: If mortgage rates fall, what will happen to inventory?
posts.summary: A poll asking what happens to housing inventory if mortgage rates fall below 6% produced no consensus: 44% predicted inventory would rise, 30% said it would fall, and 25% expected no change. Analysis of seven rate-decline periods since 1982 shows rates only correlate with inventory during weak growth periods, with inconsistent results. Evidence suggests falling rates will likely lower inventory, as they stimulate buyer demand more than seller listings.
posts.text:
This article was written by Aziz Sunderji, Principal and Chief Economist at Home Economics, and Mike Simonsen, Chief Economist at Compass, the largest residential real estate brokerage in the United States by sales volume.

A few weeks ago, we posted a poll on X.com. It split the community. The question: What's your expectation for housing inventory if mortgage rates fall persistently below 6% in the next year?

The results revealed no consensus: 44% predicted inventory would rise, 30% said it would fall, and 25% expected no change.

Credible arguments on all sides

Those who argue lower rates will raise inventory primarily cite the release of mortgage rate "lock-in." Millions of homeowners hold mortgages below prevailing rates, finding it punitive to list their homes and sacrifice that advantage. As rates fall, the thinking goes, this penalty diminishes—and the resulting surge of sellers would overwhelm any concurrent rise in demand.

The opposing camp argues that while lower rates may indeed ease lock-in and boost listings, the concurrent rise in demand will prove larger. The net effect: falling inventory.

A third camp emphasizes economic context. They argue that what happens to inventory as mortgage rates fall depends on the economic context: if growth is weakening, the drop in demand will dominate and inventory will rise. But if the move in rates is a response to cooling inflation rather than weaker growth, then the rise in demand could outpace the rise in listings, pres

posts.title: Is Atlanta Really a Commuter's Nightmare?
posts.summary: The article investigates whether Atlanta's notorious traffic congestion is causing a migration exodus. Data confirms Atlanta has the second-longest car commutes nationally (after Washington DC), with times increasing over the past decade. However, despite long commutes, Atlantans report relatively low stress and above-average happiness while commuting, suggesting their commutes are time-consuming but psychologically less taxing than other major cities.
posts.text:
The Home Economics team often encounters media reports about American housing—migration patterns, price changes, deteriorating affordability—that lack empirical support.

Whether due to deadlines, limited expertise, or inconvenient data, these oversights fail readers—especially housing professionals who need accurate information for their work.

Sometimes reporters craft false narratives; more often, they simply present claims without evidence, leaving readers unable to verify what's true. The data to test these assertions almost always exists—so why not show it?

With this article we introduce a new series: Home Economics Investigates.

Articles under this banner will examine housing-related pieces from prominent newspapers—the New York Times and Wall Street Journal will likely provide substantial fodder—and test whether reporters' assertions hold up to empirical scrutiny.

This week we investigate the Wall Street Journal's "Atlanta's Growth Streak Has Come to an End" by Cameron McWhirter and Konrad Putzier.

The article's thrust: Atlanta's decades-long growth streak has ended with its first net loss of domestic migrants in 30 years, driven by notorious traffic congestion that inspired the saying "Atlanta is exactly an hour away from Atlanta."

This commuting nightmare is pushing residents to smaller cities like Chattanooga, where relocators marvel at manageable traffic ("It's almost laughable when they talk about traffic here," one mover said).

Is the narrative accurate?

posts.title: Inventory Warning Signs for 6 Cities
posts.summary: The post asks whether inventory can predict price movements in specific cities, not just nationally. Analysis of the 60 largest U.S. cities finds that inventory changes measured over 26 months best predict current prices (R-squared of 0.62), with prices falling when supply increases by 1.68 months. Six cities—Seattle, Nashville, Memphis, Austin, New Orleans, and Raleigh—are at risk of price declines within one year based on current inventory trajectories.
posts.text:
We know that inventory predicts prices.

Last week, we showed that once national housing supply exceeds 5.8 months, prices begin to fall—typically with a 9-month delay.

But national models only go so far. Most housing professionals—whether investors, developers, or brokers—don’t operate in “the U.S. market.” They operate in specific cities, where dynamics can be wildly different.

Can inventory still predict price movements at the local level?

It turns out, yes—but modeling the relationship at sub-national level—as we do here, across the largest 60 cities—requires a different approach.

This is partly because we don't have an extensive history of local-level inventory going back more than a decade.

But it's also due to the wide variation in inventory levels and their effects across cities.

Take Austin, for example: the city saw a sharp price correction in 2022–23, even though inventory was just over 1 month of sales—an unusually low level to trigger that kind of decline((Lance Lambert of ResiClub recently pointed this out here)).

Austin prices and inventory

Meanwhile, Houston—with almost 5 months of supply today—remains a relatively hot market.

The relationship between prices and inventory is simply too heterogeneous across markets to apply the same method we used to link inventory and prices at the national level.

posts.title: When Should We Worry About Rising Inventory?
posts.summary: The post asks at what inventory level the housing market shifts from tight to soft and how quickly prices respond. Data shows that 5.0 months of inventory is the threshold—below it, inventory weakly predicts price changes, but above it, prices decline about 9 months later. The model achieves an R² of 0.75, explaining most price variation, and predicts year-over-year declines once inventory exceeds 5.81 months.

posts.title: Using Income Changes to Forecast Home Prices by County
posts.summary: The post asks which counties are under or overvalued based on income growth. Using 2019-2023 data, it finds a strong relationship between income and home price changes across large counties (R² of 36%). Counties like Brooklyn and San Francisco underperformed their income growth, while Lee County, FL and Fort Bend County, TX massively overperformed, suggesting price reversions in 2025.
posts.text:
We use the strong association between income growth and home price appreciation to identify counties that are under and overvalued.

Our prior work at Home Economics has identified income growth as one of the most important determinants of home prices((see 'Why is Housing so Expensive, here)). We have used this finding to argue, for example, that the ‘Housing Crisis’ is driven primarily by rising and increasingly unequal incomes, especially in large cities.

We now use this finding in another capacity: to identify parts of the country where home prices have not risen as much as we might have expected, based on strong income appreciation, or where they are now likely to stagnate, having appreciated more than is justified by incomes.

There is strong empirical and academic evidence for using changes in income to predict changes in home prices.

Abraham & Hendershott (1996), analysing U.S. metropolitan areas, estimated that a one-percentage-point rise in real income growth lifts prices by about 0.28 percentage points in the same year and a further 0.56 pp in the following year—roughly two-thirds of the adjustment arriving with a one-to-two-year lag.

Oikarinen (2009) finds a similar pattern for Finland: only ~20 % of the long-run adjustment shows up within the first year, and ~35 % within two years, confirming that price responses to income shocks are sluggish but predictable.

posts.title: Pricing Amenities—A Case Study: In-unit Laundry in New York City Rentals
posts.summary: How much does in-unit laundry increase rental prices for Upper West Side apartments? Using hedonic pricing analysis on 91 one-bedroom units, the study finds that apartments with in-unit laundry rent for approximately 15% more than comparable units without. For a typical $5,000/month apartment, this translates to a $500-750 monthly premium.
posts.text:
In this case study, we apply a hedonic pricing model to estimate the value of in-unit laundry in rental apartments on the Upper West Side of New York City. Our analysis finds that apartments with in-unit laundry rent for approximately 15% more than comparable units without. This premium suggests that investing in laundry facilities could yield substantial returns for landlords and developers.

Pricing the value of an amenity—a skylight, mature trees, ductless air-conditioning, or in our case today—in-unit laundry in a rental apartment—presents some unique challenges.

For one, every home is a bundle of amenities that are inseparable in the deed or rental contract. Each individual amenity is not explicitly priced((except perhaps with some amenities in new construction)).

Second, those amenities are not sold or leased on an item by item basis—you take the whole home, with all of its amenities, or none of it((in economic terms, housing is “lumpy”)). The smallest tradable clip is the entire dwelling. You can’t buy a home at a discount by forgoing the view.

Third, while some amenities are easily compared, many are not. How should we value the soft, yellow light in Southern California compared to the bright, clear light in Maine?

posts.title: Gross Cap Rates by MSA
posts.summary: The post asks how gross cap rates (rental income relative to purchase price) vary across major U.S. metros to help investors identify the best single-family rental opportunities. Data shows Western metros average 5.7% cap rates while Southern and Northeastern metros average 7.7-7.8%, with tech hubs like San Jose (3.4%) and San Francisco (3.6%) offering the lowest yields and secondary markets like McAllen (9.9%) and Syracuse (10.7%) offering the highest.
posts.text:
Gross cap rate—the ratio of rent to purchase price—remains the cleanest single-metric screen for single-family rental (SFR) strategy. We here calculate that ratio for the largest U.S. metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs), using matched price and rent data for a representative single-family asset.

The exercise is intentionally spare. By stripping out operating costs, leverage and tax effects we obtain a yield that is comparable across markets and cycle dates. The resulting MSA-level yield surface should allow capital allocators to rank markets by headline yield so underwriting hours are deployed where spreads are widest—and withheld where they are already fully priced.

This work is the first foray into a report we hope to formalize over the coming months (and to be released to paying subscribers only): a regular, data-laden snapshot of cap rates across the country.

Unlike Chicago and Miami, Houston avoids domestic out-migration.
