posts.title: The ultimate productivity hack
posts.summary: The post asks why people feel perpetually busy despite having more free time, and whether productivity hacks help. Research shows roughly one in ten people are happiest—those feeling neither rushed nor bored. The author suggests the Pomodoro Technique (25-minute work blocks) helps by making infinite tasks feel finite, reducing the feeling of being rushed and potentially increasing happiness.
posts.text:
Sunderji’s Law

Any child of immigrant entrepreneurs knows the true meaning of hard work. My parents worked around the clock, six days a week, running a chain of hearing clinics in Canada—until they sold the business and retired in 2008. These days their lives are tranquil and calm—full of oil painting, bird watching, and meditation.

Just kidding. Here is the opening of pretty much every call home:

Aziz: “Hi Dad how are you?”Dad: “We are just…so busy. So many things to do!”Aziz: “Well, hopefully when you retire you’ll be able to relax a bit”Dad: “Yes, very funny!”

Only a couple of years ago—when I left the corporate world to figure out my career 2.0—did I come to understand what my dad is going through. I went from working 11 hours a day, five days a week, for fourteen years—to having no boss, no deliverables and, at a stretch, doing something resembling “work” for a mere 11 hours a month. Yet, I felt as busy as ever.

Just as my dad replaced the time he used to spend negotiating leases with going to the gym—and felt equally busy, since one “to-do” seamlessly replaced another—I substituted reading and playing tennis for the long hours I used to spend working on spreadsheets. These new activities, if more enjoyable, still felt as urgent.

It seems to me that Parkinson’s Law (“work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion”) has a corollary (Sunderji’s Law?), which might go something like, “available time finds work to fill it”.

posts.title: Social media is the best and the worst
posts.summary:
# Summary

The post asks whether social media actually makes us unhappy or if we're just weak-willed. While academic research shows social media causes stress, loneliness, and anxiety, two experiments found that quitting Facebook for one week or one month had minimal effects on overall well-being, productivity, or happiness—and participants actually valued social media more after quitting it.
posts.text:
New Year’s resolutions experiments

I’ve never been good at New Year’s resolutions. Aside from my utter lack of willpower, it seems that I tend to adopt resolutions that don’t make me feel as good as I thought they would. I almost always drop them before the end of January.

In his book Stumbling on Happiness, psychologist Dan Gilbert argues that this is pretty normal. People are bad at forecasting what will make them happy:

“We treat our future selves as though they were our children, spending most of the hours of most of our days constructing tomorrows that we hope will make them happy... But our temporal progeny are often thankless. We toil and sweat to give them just what we think they will like, and they quit their jobs, grow their hair, move to or from San Francisco, and wonder how we could ever have been stupid enough to think they’d like that. We fail to achieve the accolades and rewards that we consider crucial to their well-being, and they end up thanking God that things didn’t work out according to our shortsighted, misguided plan.”Daniel Gilbert, Stumbling on Happiness

So this year I am acknowledging the folly of throwing myself into arbitrary resolutions, and trying something different: I am going to do some experiments. Most of these experiments probably won’t move the needle on my happiness, but maybe some will—and maybe, after experiencing their positive effects, I will be more likely to keep them going.

posts.title: We are all flawed thinking machines
posts.summary:
# Summary

The post asks which is more probable: Linda is a bank teller, or Linda is a bank teller active in feminism. Most people incorrectly answer the latter because vivid narratives override statistical thinking. The post then explains how Alex Berenson exploits Simpson's Paradox—a statistical phenomenon where trends reverse when data is disaggregated—to claim vaccinated English adults under 60 die at twice the rate of unvaccinated people, misleading readers by conflating age and vaccination effects.
posts.text:
Aziz Sunderji is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts right in your inbox (for free!), consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

I know I said I would write about market efficiency this week. I am working on it, and it’ll be a doozie, trust me. But in the meantime, please consider this interesting scenario1 and the accompanying question:

Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations.Which is more probable?a. Linda is a bank teller.b. Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.

Since you subscribe to my newsletter, you are clearly a smart, numerate person. You answered correctly (a).

But, the majority of people answer incorrectly (b).

The reason is that we confuse vividness for probability. It means that—even as we add qualifiers that make something less likely (Linda is not merely a bank teller, she is also active in the feminist movement)—we perceive it as more likely, because the image it conjures in our minds is more vivid.

Humans don’t think naturally in statistical terms. We think in stories.

posts.title: How to invest
posts.summary: In 2008, bond strategist Aziz Sunderji considered buying Lehman Brothers senior bonds that seemed underpriced, but an expert told him they were safe. Lehman collapsed weeks later, wiping out bondholders. Sunderji concludes that markets are highly efficient—prices are almost always correct, and trying to exploit pricing deviations is futile.
posts.text:
It’s late summer, 2008. I am 28 years old, two years into my job at Barclays investment bank in London. I am a bond strategist (a bond is basically a tiny slice of a huge loan to a company; investors in the bond market trade these slices with each other). My role is to advise the bank’s clients—big investors like pension funds, governments, hedge funds, and mutual funds—about which bonds they should buy in European markets.

I am feeling pretty fancy. I casually say things like, “we’re pretty bullish, spreads should tighten in the near term”. I wear a suit to work (I have exactly one suit). My desk is on the bank’s trading floor. I spend my days analyzing data, writing reports, messaging with clients, and talking to the traders and salespeople sitting next to me. Markets are wobbling; the S&P 500 soars by 5% one day only to fall by twice that amount the next day. It’s clear to me that something weird is going on, but I have utterly no clue how bad it will get.

Amid the noise, I notice that one particular bond, issued by the prestigious American investment bank Lehman Brothers, is trading at unusually depressed levels. Moreover, this is a “senior” bond—the safest kind, since Lehman Brothers will repay the senior bondholders before anyone else, including those holding riskier “junior” bonds. posts.title: The Difference between Hamilton and Healthcare
posts.summary: The post asks why healthcare and education costs have soared while the bottom 40% of households saw no income gains in 40 years, making these essentials unaffordable like luxury goods. Common explanations—administrative bloat, amenities arms races, insurance profits, malpractice costs—don't hold up; malpractice represents only $12 of $10,000 annual per-person healthcare spending. The author suggests "Baumol's cost disease" offers the real answer.

Anyone who has spent more than ten seconds hanging out with me in the past few months knows that I’ve got some bones to pick with the American version of capitalism. But…I also like to buy stuff! And there is no better place in the world to be a consumer than the US, and New York City in particular.

This is in no small part because of New York’s full-throated embrace of the price-based rationing mechanism, which dictates that if you really want something and have the cash to pay for it, in this city, it’s yours.

As economist Greg Mankiw controversially spelled out in the New York Times, it’s the ruthlessness of the price mechanism that allowed his family to see the hit Broadway musical Hamilton on short notice:

posts.title: Why is the labor market so broken?
posts.summary: Why can't workers find jobs and companies find workers despite high unemployment? The post examines two popular explanations—skills mismatch and the "Great Resignation"—but finds neither is supported by data. High unemployment and job openings coexist across the same sectors (like hotels/food), and resignation stories focus on professionals while most job openings are in other industries.
posts.text:
Odd things are happening the labor market: both unemployment and job openings are high. In other words, workers can’t seem to find jobs, and companies can’t seem to find workers.

This is not normal. Usually, after an economic setback like the one we have lived through over the past year, the labor market heals in three stages.

First, the number of people who are seeking work but can’t find it—the unemployment rate—declines. Second, stronger business conditions lead companies to post more job openings. This relationship between unemployment and openings—graphically described by the “Beveridge curve”—is shown in the historical data above.

Third, as the business cycle ages and the labor market tightens (demand exceeds supply), people feel more confident about their financial situation, and in their prospects for better work. More people start to quit.

The puzzle today is that workers are quitting and companies are finding it hard to fill openings—things that happen when the economy is strong and workers are hard to find—but all of this is taking place against a backdrop of still-high unemployment.

Shouldn’t companies be able to find workers to fill openings if so many are unemployed? And why are so many people quitting their jobs when the economy is so weak?
